operator_plays.name: DNS/Script Technographic Drop-Off & Renewal-Window Interception
operator_plays.mechanism: Crawl target commercial domains and DNS TXT/CNAME records weekly to detect the exact day a company installs or removes high-ticket enterprise software tags (Salesforce, HubSpot, Marketo, Segment, NetSuite), predicting annual renewal windows (Month 10–11) and active vendor migrations.
inputs: Weekly HTTP script-tag, DOM header, & DNS TXT/CNAME technographic crawler
Historical install-timestamp ledger (calculating 12-month contract renewal windows)
B2B executive contact graph & migration-agency/SaaS partner routing
workflow: Scan 500,000+ target B2B domains weekly for JavaScript SDKs, tracking pixels, and SPF/CNAME records of $20k–$150k/yr SaaS platforms
Flag accounts entering Month 10 of their annual contract (60 days before auto-renewal lock-in) or accounts running dual competing tags during a live evaluation
Route renewal-window and active-churn signals to competing SaaS sales teams, software resellers, and implementation agencies
metrics: Install/drop detection precision (%) and renewal-date accuracy
Outbound reply-to-demo conversion rate on Month-10 renewal targets
Per-opportunity bounty or retainer revenue per agency/SaaS partner

platform_risks.failure_mode: WAF/Cloudflare bot-blocking or false-positive tag detection from server-side GTM
platform_risks.trigger: High-concurrency crawling from datacenter IPs or misinterpreting server-side tag manager consolidation as vendor churn
platform_risks.impact: Incomplete technographic diffs or wasted sales outreach on false churn signals
platform_risks.detection_metric: Crawler HTTP 200 success rate and multi-signal verification (DNS SPF/CNAME + careers-page job-posting confirmation)
platform_risks.fallback: Combine passive DNS TXT/CNAME monitoring with job-posting technographic mentions to confirm true vendor switches before routing

Enterprise recruiting, specialty finance, & B2B agency deal-routing desk

Extract Form D issuers raising $2M–$50M (who immediately deploy capital on hiring, growth agencies, and software) and Form 8-K executive transitions
Deliver tailored briefings to the filing officers and route warm introductions to executive search firms, enterprise software resellers, and B2B agencies
metrics: EDGAR publication-to-enrichment latency (seconds)
Form D / 8-K executive response rate vs. cold baseline (3–5x lift)
Retainer and placement referral fees generated per 100 filings

platform_risks.failure_mode: SEC EDGAR automated-access block or Reg D general-solicitation confusion

platform_risks.impact: Temporary IP block by Akamai/SEC infrastructure

operator_plays.name: Subsidized / Developer-Tenant Multi-Inbox Cold Outbound Infrastructure
operator_plays.mechanism: Provisioning hundreds of isolated secondary domains across subsidized Microsoft 365 developer/partner tenants, Cloudflare Email Routing, and low-cost SMTP relays—sending strictly 15–25 plain-text emails per inbox per day across 300+ free/subsidized mailboxes to deliver 150,000+ monthly B2B cold emails into primary inboxes without paying $6–$12/seat retail Google Workspace pricing.
inputs: Lookalike secondary domain portfolio with automated SPF, DKIM (2048-bit), DMARC (`p=quarantine`/`reject`), and custom tracking-free MX records
Subsidized M365 partner/developer tenants, Cloudflare Email Routing catch-alls, and distributed SMTP sending nodes
Automated peer-to-peer warmup network and master unibox reply-routing webhook
workflow: Provision 100–300 secondary sending domains and bind 2–3 mailboxes per domain via automated DNS and tenant scripts
Warm every mailbox for 14–21 days with realistic thread-depth conversations before introducing live outbound prospects
Cap daily outbound volume at <=20 zero-link, zero-tracking-pixel plain-text messages per mailbox per day to stay completely beneath ESP volume heuristics
Aggregate all prospect replies into a single unified AI-triaged inbox that books qualified B2B sales calls on pay-per-show or retainer terms

operator_plays.name: Employer Self-Funded ERISA Plan International Specialty-Drug Importation Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Contracting with mid-market US employers (100–5,000 employees) operating self-funded ERISA health plans to carve out high-cost specialty biologics and GLP-1s ($6,000–$15,000/mo US PBM list price) and source the identical manufacturer-sealed drugs from licensed Tier-1 pharmacies in Canada, the UK, Australia, and New Zealand at $800–$2,200/mo—waiving the employee's copay to $0 while taking 25–35% of the employer's $50,000–$100,000/yr per-patient savings.
inputs: Department of Labor (DOL) Form 5500 Schedule A/C database identifying self-funded ERISA employers by broker, TPA, and stop-loss carrier
Licensed international pharmacy dispensation network across Tier-1 jurisdictions (Canada, UK, Australia, New Zealand) with cold-chain courier logistics
Turnkey ERISA Summary Plan Description (SPD) 'Specialty Drug Carve-Out Amendment' and $0-copay patient concierge portal
workflow: Mine DOL Form 5500 filings to target CFOs and benefits directors of self-funded companies with 150–3,000 covered lives
Audit the employer's anonymized pharmacy claims file to flag the 1–3% of members driving 45–60% of total drug spend (Humira, Stelara, Skyrizi, Dupixent, Enbrel, Ozempic)
Plug in a voluntary $0-copay international personal-importation program alongside the existing TPA, fulfilling 90-day cold-chain prescriptions at 60–80% below US PBM prices
Bill the self-funded employer plan a shared-savings contingency fee equal to 25–35% of verified net claim reduction ($15,000–$30,000/yr per enrolled specialty patient)
metrics: Verified annual specialty-claim savings ($) per self-funded employer group
Net shared-savings fee revenue ($15k–$30k/yr) per enrolled specialty patient
Employee $0-copay opt-in conversion rate (target: >85%)

platform_risks.failure_mode: Incumbent PBM rebate-contract retaliation or cold-chain customs shipment delay
platform_risks.trigger: Legacy PBM threatening to withhold formulary rebates if specialty scripts are carved out, or border clearance delays on temperature-sensitive biologics
platform_risks.impact: Delayed employer onboarding or need for local emergency bridge fills
platform_risks.detection_metric: Cold-chain transit temperature telemetry and net employer savings after accounting for any forfeited PBM rebates
platform_risks.fallback: Target independent TPAs and transparent pass-through PBMs first, combine international sourcing with US Manufacturer Patient Assistance Program (PAP) optimization, and maintain domestic bridge-fill coverage

operator_plays.name: 340B Contract-Pharmacy & Covered-Entity Drug Price Spread Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Partnering with HRSA-qualified 340B Covered Entities (Federally Qualified Health Centers, Ryan White clinics, disproportionate-share rural hospitals) to provide turnkey Third-Party Administrator (TPA) split-billing software, specialty contract-pharmacy fulfillment, and tele-referral capture—buying outpatient specialty medications at 25–50%+ statutory 340B discounts while collecting 100% full commercial insurance reimbursement and splitting the multi-thousand-dollar per-script margin via compliant flat administrative/dispensing fees.
inputs: HRSA OPAIS (Office of Pharmacy Affairs Information System) database of Covered Entities and registered contract pharmacies
340B split-billing / virtual-inventory accumulator software tracking 11-digit NDCs, prescriber NPIs, and patient-eligibility encounters
Licensed specialty/mail-order contract pharmacy network and commercial payer PBMs
workflow: Identify under-monetized 340B Covered Entities (FQHCs, grantees, rural hospitals) with low specialty capture rates in the HRSA OPAIS registry
Deploy split-billing TPA software and mail-order specialty contract-pharmacy infrastructure that captures commercially insured prescriptions written or co-managed by clinic providers
Reimburse the pharmacy at full commercial payer rates ($3,000–$12,000/script) while replenishing drug inventory via the clinic's 340B wholesaler account at $800–$4,000/script
Charge fixed fair-market-value per-dispense administrative, software, and clinical-management fees that capture a major share of the net spread while funding the clinic's safety-net mission
metrics: Captured commercially insured 340B scripts per month per Covered Entity
Gross commercial-to-340B acquisition spread ($1,500–$6,000+) per specialty fill
HRSA audit pass rate (zero duplicate Medicaid discount or diversion findings)

platform_risks.failure_mode: Manufacturer contract-pharmacy restriction policies or HRSA 'patient definition' audit findings
platform_risks.trigger: Drug manufacturers restricting 340B replenishment to a single contract pharmacy unless claims data is submitted, or filling scripts for patients without a documented clinic encounter
platform_risks.impact: Loss of 340B ceiling price on specific NDCs or HRSA repayment liability
platform_risks.detection_metric: 100% EHR encounter-to-NPI match verification prior to 340B replenishment accumulation and automated ESP (340B ESP) data submission
platform_risks.fallback: Operate an in-house entity-owned specialty pharmacy location alongside contract pharmacies, automate 340B ESP claims-data uploads to unlock restricted NDCs, and enforce strict EHR encounter gates

operator_plays.name: Section 321 "De Minimis" & Border Bonded-Warehouse Tariff Split-Shipping Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Routing bulk sea/air container imports for high-tariff DTC and marketplace brands into Tijuana (IMMEX) or Canadian border-zone bonded 3PL warehouses instead of US ports, then fulfilling individual US consumer orders across the border daily under 19 U.S.C. § 1321 (Section 321 Entry Type 86)—legally eliminating 15%–42.5% customs duties on qualifying consumer parcels and charging brands 35–50% of the saved tariff bill plus 3PL fulfillment fees.
inputs: USITC Harmonized Tariff Schedule (HTS) database cross-referenced against US Customs Bill-of-Lading import records (ImportYeti / Panjiva / Datamyne)
Nearshore Mexican IMMEX or Canadian customs-bonded fulfillment center 5–15 miles from San Ysidro/Otay Mesa or Windsor/Blaine border crossings
Automated CBP ACE Entry Type 86 manifest software transmitting 10-digit HTS and consignee data per individual consumer parcel
workflow: Scrape public maritime Bill-of-Lading records to identify US apparel, footwear, luggage, and consumer-goods brands importing 20+ containers/yr in 18%–37.5% HTS duty brackets
Divert the client's ocean containers in-bond (IT/T&E bond) directly to the nearshore border-zone fulfillment facility without paying US bulk entry duties
Sync the warehouse WMS with the brand's Shopify/Amazon store so each US consumer order (<$800 retail value, 1 per person per day) is picked, packed, and cleared via CBP Entry Type 86 at $0 duty
Line-item bill the brand for standard pick-and-pack fulfillment plus a 35–50% contingency split of the verified customs duties eliminated
metrics: Annualized customs duty eliminated ($500k–$10M+/yr per enterprise brand client)
Net tariff-savings share + 3PL margin ($) per parcel cleared across the border
CBP Type 86 automated release rate (>99.4%) and border transit time (<6 hours to USPS/FedEx domestic injection)

platform_risks.failure_mode: Statutory exclusion of specific Section 301 country-of-origin SKUs from Section 321 de minimis eligibility
platform_risks.trigger: Executive/statutory rulemaking removing China-origin Section 301 HTS codes from Entry Type 86 eligibility or tightening 10-digit HTS description rules
platform_risks.impact: Loss of Section 321 duty exemption on affected country-of-origin SKUs
platform_risks.detection_metric: Real-time HTS + Country-of-Origin eligibility screen in the WMS before container booking
platform_risks.fallback: Focus on non-301 origin goods (Vietnam, India, EU, Bangladesh, Cambodia) where high MFN duties (16%–32% on apparel/footwear/textiles) remain 100% Section 321 exempt, and pair with CBP First-Sale Valuation for remaining SKUs

operator_plays.name: CBP "First-Sale Rule" (19 CFR § 152.103) Multi-Tier Customs Valuation Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Restructuring multi-tiered import supply chains under the US Court of Appeals *Nissho Iwai* 'First Sale Rule' so US importers legally declare the lower factory-to-middleman transaction price ($8) for US Customs duty and tariff calculation rather than the middleman-to-US-importer invoice price ($18)—slashing annual tariff cash outflows by 35–55% across $10M–$250M+ in imported merchandise.
inputs: US Customs bill-of-lading and HTS duty-spend intelligence identifying mid-market importers paying $1M–$20M/yr in duties via trading companies
Three-party contract, factory cost-sheet, and arm's-length transfer-pricing documentation templates satisfying CBP *Nissho Iwai* criteria
Licensed customs brokerage and trade-attorney opinion pipeline
workflow: Identify US importers purchasing finished goods through Hong Kong, Singapore, Taiwanese, or European trading intermediaries or sourcing agents
Audit the two-tier transaction chain to confirm (1) bona fide sale from factory to middleman, (2) clear designation for US export at factory order, and (3) arm's-length pricing
Implement compliant multi-tier invoicing and ERP documentary trails so the customs broker declares the factory's First-Sale price on CBP Form 7501 instead of the middleman's marked-up invoice
Collect a 25–35% contingency fee on all prospective and retroactive (Post-Summary Correction / Protest) duty reductions realized by the importer
metrics: Percentage reduction in declared customs dutiable value (typically 30–50%)
Annualized cash tariff savings ($300k–$5M+/yr per importer) and retroactive PSC refund recovery ($)
CBP CF-28/CF-29 Request for Information audit survival rate (100% documentary compliance)

platform_risks.failure_mode: CBP disallowance of First-Sale valuation during a CF-28 Request for Information audit
platform_risks.trigger: Related-party factory/middleman entities failing to prove arm's-length profit margins or refusing to disclose factory commercial invoices
platform_risks.impact: Re-assessment of duties on the second-sale price plus interest
platform_risks.detection_metric: Annual pre-audit verification of factory commercial invoices, bank wire proofs, and OECD transfer-pricing benchmark studies
platform_risks.fallback: Store encrypted factory invoices in a confidential customs-broker escrow vault (so the US buyer never sees the middleman's margin, while CBP auditors have full access) and back every program with a formal customs-counsel opinion letter

operator_plays.mechanism: Embedding a 'Free Automated Accounts Payable (AP) / Instant Vendor Settlement' platform inside high-volume B2B verticals (freight brokerage, construction general contracting, medical supply, property management, media agencies) that converts checks and ACH payables into single-use Visa/Mastercard Commercial Virtual Credit Cards (VCCs)—capturing 140–195 basis points (1.40%–1.95%) in uncapped commercial interchange rebates on hundreds of millions in third-party invoice volume.

operator_plays.mechanism: Operating a wholesale high-risk Independent Sales Organization (ISO) and smart payment-orchestration gateway across 25–60 domestic and offshore acquiring banks for verticals banned by Stripe/PayPal (telehealth GLP-1s/peptides, nutra subscriptions, sweepstakes gaming, high-ticket coaching, AI companions)—buying wholesale processing at ~2.10% and charging merchants 5.50%–8.90% + rolling reserves while automatically cascading declines and deflecting pre-dispute chargebacks.

chapters.question_prompt: What is a value-added reseller, how does it differ from an MSP, and what separates VARs that win from those that stall?
chapters.title: The VAR Business Model
chapters.subtitle: VAR vs. MSP roles, choosing an ERP or vendor partner, ISV engagement asks from VARs, carrier and TMS reseller programs, customer success hand-offs, customer case studies, and what high-performing resellers do before marketing
chapters.executive_summary: VAR operators agree the license is a thin-margin entry ticket and the money sits in implementation, training, customization and support layered on top. Positive Results says most software providers push over 80 percent of sales through VARs and pay the VAR directly, while Phil Morettini warns VARs will not create demand for a vendor. Steve Preda's XAPT case shows the upside of verticalizing a commodity Microsoft ERP: $24 million in revenue and $14 million pre-tax profit, near 60 percent margin. TC2's Ben Fox details how markups hide in shaved OEM discounts and buried fees, and Stuart Sutton lays out a full license stack of setup fees, monthly minimums, usage pricing and per-hour customization. The friction points: Scott Alan Miller says a VAR's sales incentive overrides any advisory role, and Sheldon Needle flags small, high-turnover VARs.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The operators converge on one blunt definition: a VAR resells someone else's platform bundled with the labor that makes it work. Jim Ward, CEO of BrainSell, says his firm sells software platforms and adds value by supplying training, implementation, development and business-application know-how, because vendors build good software but are not on the ground day to day with its hard parts [Y3mGiwmy2l0 @ 00:01:19]. His line: software is stupid and needs to be told what to do, so the VAR maps it onto people and process. Jillian Craig of Eye on Tech lists the add-on forms as customization, additional offerings, installation, and consulting or design, and warns that small VARs often get pushed into buying through a two-tier distribution model instead of direct [WEqXH4PuF8c @ 00:00:20]. Sheldon Needle of CTS Guides frames VARs as independent companies reselling a vendor's software under license, becoming the party that sells, installs and trains the user [2tRDmrgGASk @ 00:00:00]. Steve Preda traces the model to the early 90s, when SAP, Microsoft and Oracle dominated, smaller developers struggled to sell, and system integrators began earning money by customizing, training and consulting around those platforms, taking a small margin on the license and bundling all services on top [5n6g3xVFV88 @ 00:02:09].

Everyone who touches the money agrees the license itself is thin and the services are the profit engine. Preda says the original VARs made a small margin on the software and sold their bundled services alongside it [5n6g3xVFV88 @ 00:02:09]. Ben Fox of TC2 calls resale good for revenue but a low-margin business, and says systems integrators and telecom carriers wax and wane on VAR services depending on whether they are chasing revenue growth or healthy margin that year [BJPNVL1CIiM @ 00:03:05]. Phil Morettini of PTM Consulting tells vendors that VARs will not be motivated solely by high product margins; what they market and sell very actively is their own high-margin services, so a product that enables those services puts the vendor in great shape with the channel [L1YsH5QkIus @ 00:01:22]. The flip side is leverage over vendors: Positive Results claims most software providers do over 80 percent of their sales through VARs, that the VAR is compensated by the software company, and that it never charges the client more on monthly user fees [z6rVTIy-FOg @ 00:02:59]. Fox adds that OEMs such as Cisco run channel strategies and prefer to transact through partners rather than directly, which makes VARs practically inevitable for enterprise buyers sourcing from many manufacturers at once [BJPNVL1CIiM @ 00:01:16].

The third point of agreement is that winners pick a narrow lane and vet the vendor hard before selling it. Ridge Consulting says low performers grab a technology, sprint into multiple segments without checking long-term fit and run short-term marketing, then scramble to survive when business and technology cycles turn; high performers run a full strategic review with vendor support, identify one segment with high strategic fit and build tactics to dominate it [NbukIA2E8Nw @ 00:00:50]. Preda's XAPT story proves the payoff: a Hungarian Microsoft ERP implementer customized Navision for one Caterpillar dealer, got referred to another, and turned heavy-equipment dealers into a global niche that Microsoft embraced, putting the firm on stage with Steve Ballmer [5n6g3xVFV88 @ 00:03:26]. Positive Results screens every partner on six factors: true cloud access from any device, functionality tested against real customer use cases rather than developer claims, easy integrations, simple user experience, a mobile-first build and world-class security [z6rVTIy-FOg @ 00:00:42]. Morettini insists the vendor, not the VAR, must position the product and create demand, and must have sold it successfully direct first so it has best practices to hand partners, because VARs will not create demand or spearhead a new marketplace for anyone [L1YsH5QkIus @ 00:02:38].

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Ben Fox of TC2 breaks down exactly how the VAR's cut gets taken, and it is rarely one clean number. The markup is the charge for VAR services, applied either as a percentage over net cost of goods or by shaving the OEM discount: if the OEM gives 60 percent off, the VAR passes through 58 [BJPNVL1CIiM @ 00:04:10]. Fox stresses that a one percent markup on cost and a one percent cut to the discount sound identical but land very differently on the final price, and that the least transparent model simply quotes a net discount per OEM so nobody sees the margin [BJPNVL1CIiM @ 00:04:42]. Markups also float by country, by OEM, and by whether a distributor sits between VAR and manufacturer, which lines up with Eye on Tech's point that small VARs get routed through two-tier distribution and only mark up the distributor's product a small amount [WEqXH4PuF8c @ 00:01:33]. Fox's checklist of fees that get buried includes import duties, customs clearance, import broker fees, exchange-rate hedging, extra logistics layers and management fees; only shipping and sales tax should ride on top [BJPNVL1CIiM @ 00:05:51]. On recurring cloud licenses, Positive Results says the vendor pays the VAR, leaving client per-user fees untouched [z6rVTIy-FOg @ 00:02:59].

Stuart Sutton's Full Circle TMS walkthrough lays out the most granular VAR license structure of any operator. Applicants must be non-transportation entities so subscribers trust their data stays away from competitors, they get a geographic area or vertical, their office must sit inside that territory, and the product is rebranded to look like theirs; the license is kept only by generating sufficient business within the first two years [yasPH-UlTQo @ 00:03:43]. The vendor bills the VAR a one-time setup and training cost, a monthly VAR fee, a wholesale price on subscriber usage, on-demand support charges above a threshold, and cost-plus-management-fee pay for any dedicated developer, who stays a Full Circle employee that the VAR cannot poach [yasPH-UlTQo @ 00:07:26]. The VAR earns back through a setup and training fee, a minimum monthly charge, module-based usage fees, paid extra training and per-hour customization work [yasPH-UlTQo @ 00:08:10]. Preda shows what customization does to price: generic Salesforce ran 25 per seat, while a firm that tailored it for investment banks charged 250 a month for the same basic package and he judged it clearly better [5n6g3xVFV88 @ 00:05:29]. XAPT later spun off its customization arm into a US-headquartered company of 450 employees, three times the original business [5n6g3xVFV88 @ 00:07:04].

The day-to-day motion runs on fast qualification, joint deals and adoption follow-through. VAR panelists at Channel Marketing Academy want vendors to hand them ballpark tiers, such as entry, medium and hard implementations at roughly a month and a half, six months and two years, because a customer who will spend $5,000 may balk at $50,000 and the VAR will not risk the embarrassment of presenting an unpriced product [vLO0gA3TgxE @ 00:02:14]. They want a 15-minute pitch and a one-page cheat sheet, not an hour-long demo. Brian Tanney of GetWireless, grown from two people in a basement to over 90 team members in 25 years, describes a VAR-led program being architected with AT&T where VARs bring deals in and either bill the hardware on their own paper or run it on AT&T paper with the buy-down showing on the customer's bill [-gG3jIROESw @ 00:03:27], alongside six state and local contracts and a GSA federal contract [-gG3jIROESw @ 00:02:42]. Atlassian's partner customer-success program checks deployment after purchase and again four months before license expiry; one quarter it flagged 20 at-risk high-volume customers, remediated eight, saved over 250,000 in revenue and lifted renewals 5 percent, and it names failure to go live in production as the top reason customers do not renew [4qYKEjVIAjc @ 00:00:57].

sections.title: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The money question splits the field. Positive Results tells buyers flatly that value-added resellers never charge more for monthly user fees because the VAR is compensated by the software company, and claims most software providers do over 80 percent of their sales through VARs [z6rVTIy-FOg @ 00:02:59]. Eye on Tech frames it the other way: VARs mark up the distributor's product a small amount and cannot control the cost of what they sell [WEqXH4PuF8c @ 00:01:33]. Ben Fox of TC2, speaking on Staying Connected, treats the markup as the actual charge for VAR services and splits it into two mechanics: a straight percentage on the net cost of goods, or a quiet haircut to the OEM discount, where a 60 percent OEM discount becomes 58 percent by the time it reaches the buyer [BJPNVL1CIiM @ 00:04:10]. Fox stresses that the two sound identical yet hit the invoice differently, and that the least transparent VARs simply quote a net discount per OEM with no visible markup. Full Circle TMS, pitched by Stuart Sutton, runs a fourth model: the vendor bills the VAR a wholesale price and expects the VAR to mark up what it sells [yasPH-UlTQo @ 00:07:26].

On margins, the practitioners report opposite worlds. Steve Preda pulled the last public financials of XAPT, the Hungarian Microsoft ERP reseller founded by Zoltan Schwartz: 24 million dollars in revenue and 14 million dollars profit before tax, almost a 60 percent net margin, earned by customizing a commodity Microsoft ERP for Caterpillar and heavy equipment dealers [5n6g3xVFV88 @ 00:04:18]. Preda's read is that the margin came from inventing the customization, not the license. A second data point comes from Preda's investment banking days: a plain Salesforce seat at 25 a month versus a niche firm charging 250 a month for the same base package customized for investment banks, a 10x price point purely from vertical tailoring [5n6g3xVFV88 @ 00:05:29]. Ben Fox describes resale as the opposite: good for revenue but a low margin business, which is why systems integrators and telecom carriers wax and wane on pushing it depending on whether they are chasing growth or margin [BJPNVL1CIiM @ 00:03:05]. Eye on Tech goes further, reporting that VARs are finding it harder to stay in the market as margins, revenue and competitive positions shift, and are migrating toward an MSP role [WEqXH4PuF8c @ 00:02:13].

Identity and territory are the third fault line. Scott Alan Miller of SAM IT holds a hard line: once a VAR, always a VAR, any MSP work is just part of the value add, and a reseller presenting itself purely as an MSP is misleading to the point of being questionably ethical or legal, because the sales side is paid to represent the vendor, not the customer [bek-1YEtW80 @ 00:03:15]. Eye on Tech treats the MSP shift as a survival move rather than a disclosure problem. On customization ownership, the playbooks diverge sharply. XAPT built its own NAXT vertical layer and eventually spun the customization business into a United States company with 450 employees, roughly three times the size of the original business, per Steve Preda [5n6g3xVFV88 @ 00:07:04]. Full Circle TMS closes that path off: any dedicated developer must be a Full Circle employee or contractor billed to the VAR at cost plus a management fee, the vendor owns all IP, and the VAR cannot recruit vendor staff, though it keeps prioritization control [yasPH-UlTQo @ 00:05:49]. Ridge Consulting adds the segment question: high performers pick one segment with high strategic fit and, with vendor support, plan tactics to dominate it [NbukIA2E8Nw @ 00:01:06].

sections.title: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Phil Morettini says many software management teams get off on the wrong foot with the VAR channel, and in the worst cases it ends in failure of the company. The core trap: VARs will not create demand, will not spearhead a new marketplace, and will not be motivated solely by high product margins; they push their own high-margin services, so the product has to be the enabler of those services. Morettini's rule is that no one can sell your product if you cannot, so sell directly and successfully first, never take a sale direct to grab a few extra points, and never over-distribute by assigning too many VARs in one local area, because brutal competition strips out the profit margin and the incentive to sell [L1YsH5QkIus @ 00:03:16]. Ridge Consulting documents the reseller-side version: low performers pick a technology, grab multiple market segments without checking long-term fit, and launch short-term marketing, which works until later business and technology cycles leave them in a painful scramble to survive, if not outright disaster [NbukIA2E8Nw @ 00:00:15]. On the Channel Marketing Academy panel, a VAR states they will not even present a vendor that refuses budgetary numbers, because a 50,000 dollar surprise to a 5,000 dollar client is embarrassing [vLO0gA3TgxE @ 00:02:14].

Operational traps hit both buyers and VARs. Sheldon Needle of CTS Guides warns that VARs are often small organizations with heavy turnover, may lack experience in your industry or in applications like EDI, CRM or HR, and some vendors will not back you up by assigning another VAR when one underperforms [2tRDmrgGASk @ 00:00:38]. The worst case is a staff change mid-project that leaves the customer high and dry. Ben Fox lists the fee leakage: import duties, customs clearance fees, import broker fees, exchange rate hedging, extra logistics layers and extra management fees, when the only costs above product plus markup should be hardware shipping and sales taxes [BJPNVL1CIiM @ 00:05:51]. Fox has seen the variation in logistics, shipping and even taxes between VARs exceed the variation in the markup itself, and has caught importation and customs fees disguised as taxes in quotes. Geographic coverage is the other trap: without an in-country entity licensed to sell the product, the customer ends up as importer of record, which defeats the purpose of hiring a VAR. Stuart Sutton's Full Circle model adds on-demand support charges once a VAR exceeds a support threshold, and pulls the license from VARs that fail to generate sufficient business within two years [yasPH-UlTQo @ 00:03:59].

Adoption is where renewals die. Atlassian's customer success team, presented by Summer Zaldivar, reports that the primary reason customers do not renew is failing to go live into production; last quarter they flagged 20 high-volume customers at risk, remediated 8 by connecting them with premier support, saved over 250,000 in revenue and lifted the renewal rate by 5 percent [4qYKEjVIAjc @ 00:00:36]. Their ask of partners is to collect feedback at purchase: deployed into production, active users, more to add, business requirements met, blockers, documentation needs; Atlassian then checks back four months before the license expires. Stuart Sutton reaches the same conclusion from the VAR seat: initial setup and training are critical to long-term subscriber success, the first few months are critical, and the VAR must keep following up until the customer runs their entire business on the platform [yasPH-UlTQo @ 00:04:31]. Sutton also tells VARs to charge a minimum monthly amount in case usage fees fall below the cost of cutting an invoice. Positive Results claims the payoff of process-first implementation: never more than a quarter percent annual attrition in over 25 years [z6rVTIy-FOg @ 00:03:18]. AT&T's Shiraz Asan reports the same pattern: when the partners work well together, customers stay much longer and do not turn away [-gG3jIROESw @ 00:02:10].

callout.title: Four Kill Switches Before You Scale the Channel
callout.body: Each gate comes straight from a practitioner-reported loss; fail any one and the channel bleeds margin, presentations, or renewals.
items: Do not launch a VAR channel until the product sells direct, because no one can sell your product if you cannot [Phil Morettini — L1YsH5QkIus @ 00:02:18].

Publish entry, medium and heavy implementation ballparks, such as a month and a half, six months and two years, or VARs will not put you in front of clients [Channel Marketing Academy — vLO0gA3TgxE @ 00:01:38].
Demand a written markup definition and a broken-out tax line on every quote so customs and import fees cannot hide under taxes [Staying Connected — BJPNVL1CIiM @ 00:08:32].
Track go-live into production and active users for every customer from purchase, since failing to go live is the primary non-renewal driver [Summer Zaldivar — 4qYKEjVIAjc @ 00:00:57].

chapters.question_prompt: How does a software vendor build, recruit for, and fund a reseller channel program that partners will actually use?
chapters.title: Building and Funding a Reseller Channel Program
chapters.subtitle: Step-by-step SaaS channel design, reseller vs. referral setups in partner portals, PRM deal registration and lead distribution with Salesforce, VMware's recruitment case study, ISV channel mistakes, recurring-commission programs, and why partners leave Market Development Funds unused
chapters.executive_summary: Operators who build reseller channels agree on two things: sequence and selectivity. Fix direct sales first. Recruit a narrow set of partners rather than 200 or 300 idle logos. Make the partner's money obvious with free training, no joining fees and tiered margins. Ted Finch's template runs authorized, gold and platinum tiers at 10/20/30% margins, with a $250K platinum quota and bonuses for deal registration. Payouts range from TAP's $2,500 a month for 12 months per sale to Ooma's majority-upfront model. Willingness to Pay prices partner payouts against a $21,500 direct CAC. MDF is chronically wasted: ZINFI cites up to 60% unused each quarter, and The Crancer Group recovered $5-7K and, in other cases, $20-50K of missed Microsoft co-op. The sharpest split is margin size. Luasai says resellers take 5-10%, while Viktor's guest says 20-30% usually is not going to be enough.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The loudest agreement among operators is about sequencing: fix the direct motion before you bolt on a channel. Luasai's founders say most ISVs hire direct reps first and end up about six months behind. They then retrofit a channel and have to 'double pay the channel and the reps' [9ijiF4Aas8o @ 00:03:22]. The Willingness to Pay consultant draws on 30+ client projects and often ends up killing the channel for clients. He warns that a partner is 'never going to be better at selling' your product than you are, so direct sales get fixed first [_pp2kmBgn7s @ 00:47:03]. Viktor from Sales reaches the same conclusion in his takeaways: figure out direct sales, get a seat at the table, do things that don't scale, and skip the PRM early [6Z4v3jibmMw @ 00:41:37]. The second shared rule is fewer, sharper partners. Luasai warns against recruiting 200 partners only to watch '195' sit idle. Viktor's guest says signing '300 Partners' in a month spreads the team too thin. He pushes a narrow ideal partner profile and fast disqualification instead [6Z4v3jibmMw @ 00:04:25]. Founders who expect gratitude get corrected too. Partners are often bigger businesses, and recruiting one is like hiring a rep on 'commission only,' so the vendor has to earn every hour of attention.

The second consensus point is that a reseller program lives or dies on one question partners ask: can I make money? Ted Finch of channel.com has worked in the channel since 1989 and built 270+ programs. He says resellers first probe whether the product is competitive, then margins, regional competition, training, channel conflict and sales tools. He discourages charging for training because it becomes a barrier to entry [hdz5UsJS-qY @ 00:05:29]. Vendors running live programs echo this low-friction entry. Iron Software's Nick pitches 'no joining fee and no upfront commitment,' plus tiered discounts where 'the more you sell, the deeper your discounts' [lCobx44k0Tw @ 00:00:47]. TAP Innovations bundles materials, resources and training 'at no extra cost.' That covers lead generation, selling to existing and past customers, opportunity meetings and account management [6_xruMdmmjM @ 00:02:40]. Ooma provides training modules, a partner support line, and a marketing and branding library. VARs also get a Dedicated Account Manager, priority technical support and the option to order direct [a299ToKLxRs @ 00:00:45]. The pattern holds across all four: enablement is free, economics are tiered to reward volume, and partners can reach support while a deal is still live. Finch adds that a reseller support hotline should answer in 30 seconds, not 20 minutes.

On market development funds, operators agree on two things: the money is real, and most partners leave it on the table. Pete Matheson calls MDF 'free money, sat there, waiting for you to use it.' It typically covers up to 50% of an activity and is usually paid after the event. He says mostly bigger MSPs tap it, while smaller ones don't know about it, don't understand it, or don't use it [lcMWkAWGxSU @ 00:00:32]. ZINFI puts a number on the leak: its worldwide channel survey data shows 'as much as 60%' of market development funds go unused each quarter [lET3Wc2a74o @ 00:00:35]. ZINFI gives several reasons. The vendor is an add-on rather than the partner's core business. Partners under $5-10M plan quarterly. Resellers lack digital skills and dedicated marketers. The Crancer Group calls Microsoft co-op the 'biggest missed incentive,' measured on CSP seats and MRR, Azure consumption, and designations or specializations [dM62o5Vq5U4 @ 00:03:10]. Marketing Business Network lays out the chain everyone works within: proposal, approval, activity, a claim with evidence, then payment. It stresses that 'an approved budget is not automatically a payment' [gPoVTzxEwPw @ 00:00:44]. ZINFI's fix is to focus on partners who already use funds and to automate localized, co-branded campaigns partners can launch themselves.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Ted Finch's tier template is the most complete build sheet any of these operators offer. Use plain names, 'authorized, gold, platinum,' with example margins of 10/20/30%. Authorized carries no quota and gets no leads. Gold adds a quota and first-level certification. Platinum's example quota is $250K a year plus a second certification covering first- and second-line support [hdz5UsJS-qY @ 00:08:53]. Leads route by region, then by level, and quotas keep a shared salesforce loyal. For the ramp, he grandfathers new partners into gold for 90 days. He runs a new program for about six months, then sets levels from real data, for example platinum at $100K-150K with a $10K minimum. Partners get three months to transition between levels [hdz5UsJS-qY @ 00:13:19]. His deal-registration split plugs into the tiers: gold gets 10% base plus 10% for registering, and platinum gets 20% base plus 10%. If registration compliance is low, he raises the registered portion. Digital Watchdog runs four tiers, with better buying discounts at higher tiers. Partners must save up to five distribution account numbers under the My Company tab before they can earn rewards [NrZYppqY_R4 @ 00:00:16]. Iron Software keeps tiered discounts without hard quotas, 'so your incentive grows with your performance' [lCobx44k0Tw @ 00:01:25].

Payout design is where the numbers get specific. TAP Innovations pays '$2,500 per month for 12 months for each sale,' and its sweet spot is organizations of 100-1,000 people [6_xruMdmmjM @ 00:02:23]. Ooma pays a multiple of monthly service plus a percentage of ongoing service. Unlike programs that dole payment out slowly over a long period, Ooma 'pays the majority upfront' [a299ToKLxRs @ 00:00:28]. Finch shows why timing matters. A $10K desktop sale pays $1,000 now, versus $100 a month on a $12K SaaS deal. SaaS can pay roughly 3x over five years. Companies at $1-5M pay 28% upfront, and larger ones pay 50%. A 70% cancellation rate makes the deal a 'bum deal' for the partner [hdz5UsJS-qY @ 00:53:21]. The Willingness to Pay consultant prices partner payouts against the CAC funnel he would otherwise fund: 100 leads at $10k, 20 qualified at $2k, 4 demos at $4k, 2 evaluations at $3k and 1 close at $2.5k. That totals $21,500 CAC, and he pays partners for the funnel stages they actually cover [_pp2kmBgn7s @ 00:13:06]. He also checks fit: your product should be 5-15% of the partner's deal. He drops the '20% of ARR' norm and front-loads payment, for example 50% in year one.

The plumbing is concrete. Channeltivity's Zach pushes partner-registered deals into Salesforce as leads. Partner data stays in separate fields 'since there's an inherent danger' in letting partners update your CRM, and the link survives conversion from lead to opportunity. Setup takes four steps: enter credentials with API access, choose deal registration only or add lead distribution, map fields in each direction, done [5iuG2nYpJ0U @ 00:00:55]. PartnerPortal io frames the reseller switch as 'who collects the customer's money.' Set the Partner Model card to Reseller and let the partner collect. Match revenue by tagging Stripe, QuickBooks or Xero invoices with the lead's website domain. For revenue with no named customer, create a catch-all Won lead on the reseller's own domain [KpcTpbw5dho @ 00:01:09]. Finch uses a generic portal until about 50 partners. His record setup time is under four hours, and he warns against replicating the main website inside the portal [hdz5UsJS-qY @ 00:15:19]. For Microsoft, The Crancer Group picks the Cloud Solutions Provider fund category, not hosting co-op. A $0 balance means either no designation or not yet past the $10K threshold. He checks every location plus hosting co-op and Surface rebates. That turned up an extra $5-7K and, in other cases, $20-50K [dM62o5Vq5U4 @ 00:06:19].

callout.title: Street-Level Moves Operators Actually Run
callout.body: Unconventional tactics operators use to filter competitors, drive real product usage, mine hidden partners and unlock incentive tiers.
items: Add a fake 'authorized distributor' requirement to the reseller application to stop competitors from applying. Pair it with detailed partner profiling; one company paid $38,000 to re-profile later [chanimalvideos — hdz5UsJS-qY @ 00:40:02].

Charge $5-10 for not-for-resale copies instead of giving them away. Ashton-Tate's free 15-per-location copies mostly went uninstalled, while a small charge pushed usage above 70%. Alternative: a 10-question quiz [chanimalvideos — hdz5UsJS-qY @ 00:37:23].

Run Clearbit enrichment on your existing user base to find partners already inside it. Viktor's guest surfaced about 700 agencies already using the product [Viktor from Sales — 6Z4v3jibmMw @ 00:07:14].

Count nonprofits toward new customer adds in Microsoft's program. They can carry a partner to the Modern Work designation, which Copilot accelerators require [The Crancer Group — dM62o5Vq5U4 @ 00:01:58].

sop_steps.title: Recruit From Competitors' Reseller Benches First
sop_steps.action: Build the recruiting list in order: competitors' resellers, then alliance partners, then purchased lists. Open with email.
sop_steps.detail: Finch starts with competitors' resellers, moves to alliance partners such as Citrix's roughly 2,200, then lists such as CMP and VAR City. He runs a 3-part email campaign. A CRN newsletter placement cost about $800 and brought in 35 resellers [chanimalvideos — hdz5UsJS-qY @ 01:03:43].

sop_steps.title: Launch Tiers With A Grandfathered Ramp
sop_steps.action: Grandfather new partners into gold for 90 days, run about six months, then set tier thresholds from actual sales data.
sop_steps.detail: Example thresholds after the ramp: platinum at $100K-150K with a $10K minimum. Give three months to transition between levels. Require one promotion per month for the first three months [chanimalvideos — hdz5UsJS-qY @ 00:13:19].

sop_steps.title: Wire Deal Registration Into The CRM
sop_steps.action: Push registered deals into Salesforce as leads with partner data walled off in separate fields, and map fields both directions.
sop_steps.detail: Enter credentials with API access, pick deal registration only or add lead distribution, and map fields for each direction. The link survives conversion from lead to opportunity [Channeltivity - Channel Partner Portal — 5iuG2nYpJ0U @ 00:00:55].

sop_steps.title: Run MDF Through The Full Claim Chain
sop_steps.action: Get the proposal approved before spending. Execute the activity, file the claim with evidence on deadline, then track outcomes separately.
sop_steps.detail: An approved budget is not automatically a payment. Miss a deadline or run unapproved spend and the partner may pay the bill. Partners may also have to front the costs [Marketing Business Network — gPoVTzxEwPw @ 00:00:44].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over how much margin a reseller actually needs. Luasai [9ijiF4Aas8o @ 00:14:38] calls the 40% objection false outright. In their enterprise deals, the distributor and the VAR combined take 5%, maximum 10%, because the ISV rep keeps control and plays quarterback on SKU and terms while the partner offloads procurement admin. Viktor from Sales [6Z4v3jibmMw @ 00:30:05] lands somewhere else. A 20 to 30% margin usually is not going to be enough on its own, because the partner's real money is in services. At 10% of a $100k deal the partner gets only $10k, so certifications, marketing and priority support have to round out the offer. chanimalvideos [hdz5UsJS-qY @ 00:47:51] brings survey data showing how fragmented the market is. Sixty percent of SaaS vendors pay 10 to 15%, which Ted Finch labels affiliate rates. Some pay 16 to 30%, and 21% pay 40% or more. Meanwhile a desktop 50% discount erodes to roughly 30% once the reseller discounts to win. Willingness to Pay [_pp2kmBgn7s @ 00:27:14] documents the high end in practice. In a hospital-robot deal the vendor ran the entire top of the funnel and the distributor only closed, yet the distributor still took 30%.

Payout timing splits operators into front-loaders and drip-payers. Willingness to Pay [_pp2kmBgn7s @ 00:35:26] tells clients to drop the 20%-of-ARR norm and front-load, for example 50% in year one, then pay cost-plus for any service work. The VC math backs this up. At ARR 100 and a 20x multiple, the front-loaded model funds roughly 200 per year of capital, versus about 160 under a recurring 20% cut. Ooma [a299ToKLxRs @ 00:00:28] pitches the same idea to recruits. Unlike most programs where payment is slowly doled out over a long period of time, Ooma pays a multiple of monthly service plus a percentage of ongoing service, with the majority upfront. TAP Innovations [6_xruMdmmjM @ 00:02:23] runs the opposite structure, paying $2,500 per month for 12 months for each sale. Its sweet spot is organizations of 100 to 1,000 people. chanimalvideos [hdz5UsJS-qY @ 00:53:21] frames the tension in cash terms. A $10K desktop sale pays the reseller $1,000 now, while a $12K SaaS deal pays $100 a month, even though SaaS can pay about three times as much over five years. Vendors at $1 to 5M pay 28% upfront and larger ones pay 50%. A 70% cancellation rate turns recurring commission into a bum deal.

Quotas and recruiting breadth are the third fault line. chanimalvideos [hdz5UsJS-qY @ 00:08:53] builds authorized, gold and platinum tiers at example margins of 10, 20 and 30%. Authorized carries no quota. Gold adds a quota and first-level certification. Platinum requires a $250K yearly quota plus a second certification. The argument is that quotas keep a shared salesforce loyal. Leads route by region and then by level, and authorized partners get none. Iron Software [lCobx44k0Tw @ 00:01:25] goes the other way: no joining fee, no upfront commitment, no hard quotas, and discounts that simply deepen the more a partner sells. On volume, chanimalvideos [hdz5UsJS-qY @ 01:03:43] recruits wide. The order is competitors' resellers first, then alliance partners such as Citrix's roughly 2,200, then purchased lists. One CRN newsletter placement cost about $800 and brought in 35 resellers. The same session cites SalesLogix pilfering over 800 resellers from GoldMine. It also recommends a fake authorized-distributor requirement to stop competitors from applying. Viktor from Sales [6Z4v3jibmMw @ 00:05:07] runs the opposite playbook. That means a narrow ideal partner profile and fast disqualification, plus a blunt warning that signing 300 partners in a month spreads the partner team too thin.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive failure is opening a channel too early or bolting it on too late. Luasai [9ijiF4Aas8o @ 00:03:22] watches ISVs hire direct reps first and land about six months behind. They then retrofit a channel and end up having to double pay the channel and the reps. Of the 10 to 20 ISVs they cite, very few get the mix right. Willingness to Pay [_pp2kmBgn7s @ 00:01:17] reports more channels failing than succeeding across 30-plus client projects and often ends up killing the channel outright. The same speaker warns [_pp2kmBgn7s @ 00:47:03] that a partner is never going to be better at selling your product than you are, so direct sales get fixed first. Viktor from Sales [6Z4v3jibmMw @ 00:01:40] adds the founder trap. Teams turn to partners only when they hit a growth ceiling, then discover several problems at once. Partners take longer to nurture than direct deals, they expect leads from the vendor too, and they often sign up for the logo and then never sell, or undercut on price. Luasai names the mindset error underneath all of it. Founders expect partners to be grateful, but partners are often bigger businesses, and recruiting one is like hiring a rep on commission only.

Partner sprawl and deal-size misfit kill programs that look healthy on paper. Luasai [9ijiF4Aas8o @ 00:25:51] warns against recruiting 200 partners with 195 sitting idle, and against importing Palo Alto playbooks into a Series A company. Viktor from Sales [6Z4v3jibmMw @ 00:36:27] recounts the big-logo version at Accenture, where roughly 100 users out of 200,000 people in India alone was not enough. Small agencies of 10 to 100 people moved faster. Willingness to Pay [_pp2kmBgn7s @ 00:21:01] puts a number on the misfit: about three of four partner agreements fail on ACV. A $200k product inside a $500k system-integrator project is too big at 40% of the deal. A $5k product adds only about 0.2% and is too small. The sweet spot is 5 to 15% of the partner's deal, roughly $25k to $75k. The same speaker tracks a partner funnel where 100 surveyed partners yield 2 closed, then watches for silent-partnership churn after signing. Recruiting itself grinds. chanimalvideos [hdz5UsJS-qY @ 00:44:53] reports a record of seven calls just to reach one channel manager, and finds that 60 to 70% of vendor sites miss sign-up basics.

Funding traps sit inside MDF and co-op mechanics. Marketing Business Network [gPoVTzxEwPw @ 00:01:41] lays out the chain: proposal, approval, activity, claim with evidence, then payment. The speaker stresses that an approved budget is not automatically a payment. With a 50% match capped at $1,000, a $1,600 event returns $800. A missed deadline or unapproved spend can leave the partner paying the whole bill. Pete Matheson [lcMWkAWGxSU @ 00:01:43] warns that some vendors demand proof of ROI, leads, conversion rates and sales. Mostly bigger MSPs claim the funds, while smaller ones don't know about them, don't understand them, or don't use them. ZINFI Technologies [lET3Wc2a74o @ 00:00:59] explains why as much as 60% of MDF goes unused each quarter. The vendor is an add-on, partners under $5 to 10M plan quarterly, and they lack dedicated marketers. Corruption sometimes reaches into channel management itself. The Crancer Group [dM62o5Vq5U4 @ 00:06:19] shows the Microsoft version of the leak. A $0 balance means no designation, or not yet past the $10K threshold. Checking every location, plus hosting co-op and Surface rebates, surfaced an extra $5 to 7K, and in other cases $20 to 50K.

callout.title: Four Kill-Switch Checks Before You Sign or Fund a Partner
callout.body: Run each check before you sign a partner or commit channel budget. Every check comes from a loss, reversal or bottleneck the practitioners hit themselves.
items: Do not open the channel until direct sales converts, because a partner is never going to be better at selling your product than you are [Willingness to Pay — _pp2kmBgn7s @ 00:47:03].
Recruit only partners you can activate, since 200 signed partners with 195 sitting idle is the pattern that sinks programs [Luasai — 9ijiF4Aas8o @ 00:25:51].

Keep partner-submitted deal data in separate CRM fields, since there's an inherent danger in letting partners update your CRM directly [Channeltivity - Channel Partner Portal — 5iuG2nYpJ0U @ 00:00:55].

Get every MDF activity approved first and file the claim with evidence before the deadline, because an approved budget is not automatically a payment [Marketing Business Network — gPoVTzxEwPw @ 00:00:44].

chapters.question_prompt: What do distributors like TD SYNNEX and Ingram Micro provide resellers, and how are marketplaces reshaping the channel?
chapters.title: Distributors, Aggregators, and the Marketplace Shift
chapters.subtitle: TD SYNNEX lifecycle and partner services, Ingram Micro Cloud and the ConnectWise billing connector, Pax8 channel skilling, AI-driven B2B commerce and partner data, cloud consumption fraud, high-growth vendor programs, and Canalys forecasts on marketplaces and partners
chapters.executive_summary: Distribution executives at TD SYNNEX, Pax8 and Ingram Micro Cloud, plus Canalys analyst Jay McBain, agree the money has moved from boxes to services and marketplaces: hardware is down to 16 percent of partner revenue, 80 to 90 percent of 1,400 surveyed partners have or plan services investment, and marketplace growth runs at 86 percent compounded. The street mechanics are billing and quoting automation: ID Sync pushes marketplace mailbox counts into ConnectWise agreements, Digital Bridge connects Autotask, ConnectWise, HubSpot, ServiceNow and QuickBooks Online, and deal registrations become quotes before the partner asks. Expansion pays: a five-day migration grew into full managed services, and a small support deal led to a $5 million-plus, 1,350-user contract. The split: distributors sell white-label delivery, while McBain says buyers now want seven named partners and no single throat to choke.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The distributors and the analyst covering them agree on one hard fact: the box alone no longer carries the business, and the money now sits in the services wrapped around it. Steven Andis, who runs technology acceleration for TD SYNNEX across Europe, frames the formula bluntly as product plus service equals solution, and says customers no longer ask for a firewall; they ask to enhance their security posture, which turns into a firewall plus assessment, implementation and rollout [ULy4t5kvUt0 @ 00:03:36]. The company's fourth Direction of Technology survey, covering 1,400 partners across 40 countries, found 80 to 90 percent of partners already have or plan to invest in services capability, with roughly 80 percent investing in managed services [ULy4t5kvUt0 @ 00:06:03]. Jay McBain of Canalys puts the same shift in revenue terms: hardware has fallen to 16 percent of the revenue mix and 13 percent of the profit mix for more than a thousand surveyed MSPs and VARs, so 84 percent of the business is now software and services [SwebwmaZR2I @ 00:02:55]. Graham Kelly of TD SYNNEX, working the InfoComm floor, says the old view of distribution as pick, pack and ship undersells what the house now does, from field services to stripping cost out of the supply chain [4HmZZT3HBnA @ 00:01:02].

The second point of agreement is that the distributor stays behind the partner, never in front of the customer. Andis calls TD SYNNEX an absolute two-tier distributor that sells services only to partners, filling gaps in competence, capability, skills or geography whether the partner covers 90 percent of the job or 10 percent, and its engineers can arrive on site wearing the partner's t-shirt [ULy4t5kvUt0 @ 00:14:41]. Mark Best, who runs European managed and support services, lists zero competition as the core pitch: the company does not sell directly and exists only to service partners [K3d3674aDZ8 @ 00:05:17]. Sophia from the same services organization backs the outsourcing math with a field example: a very large UK partner running roughly 85 percent services-led business delivers only 40 percent of those services itself and farms the other 60 percent out to over 300 providers in the UK alone, which is the management load the distributor pitches itself as the single point for [2qmTwyQCa_o @ 00:02:45]. Ben Elder at Ingram Micro Cloud UK sells the same white-label idea at level 1, with a 24/7 service desk acting as the single point of contact for end-user incidents in local languages, during whatever service hours the partner subscribes to [M5I7gKJnNwU @ 00:02:57].

Everyone on this beat also agrees that the buying surface is collapsing into marketplaces and single-pane platforms. Jay McBain tracks marketplace growth at 86 percent compounded and says Canalys predicted AWS would become a top-10 distributor by 2025, only to watch it get there by the end of 2023, with companies now announcing billion-dollar businesses run purely through AWS [3uRf7nlQ_JY @ 00:13:16]. Nikki Meyer of Pax8 describes the cloud-distributor version: the Pax8 Marketplace handles billing, quoting and provisioning of cloud products so an MSP sends the customer a single monthly bill [Ccgwwzx0ld4 @ 00:01:12]. Ingram Micro Cloud pitches the same single pane of glass, a marketplace built on the Odin service automation platform that automates billing across Microsoft CSP, McAfee SaaS, RingCentral phone systems and cloud backup, because the subscription model has replaced the old way software was sold [M5I7gKJnNwU @ 00:02:25]. TD SYNNEX's answer is StreamOne Ion, which Russell Rebane says pulls Microsoft, AWS and Google into one platform with automated billing, customer management, real-time usage insights and custom-branded storefronts [1Rg0jWCs65Y @ 00:08:57]. McBain's read on why this matters: 73 percent of the market flows indirect, so distributors are backing their reseller relationships with marketplace technology to keep the transaction there.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The plumbing behind marketplace resale is billing sync, and the vendors walk it click by click. Ingram Micro Cloud's ID Sync Billing Connector is bought inside the marketplace by logging in with IAM Online credentials, selecting the package and paying; the Billing Studio is then downloaded from the reseller control panel's ID Sync tab with a license key [ynfBBQclUKU @ 00:00:28]. After a one-time linking of marketplace accounts to ConnectWise agreements, the studio shows every customer's subscriptions and resource counts, such as two of ten 1 GB basic mailboxes in use; provision a third mailbox, hit force update, and ConnectWise logs a one-count adjustment on the agreement, spreadsheet free [ynfBBQclUKU @ 00:03:22]. Russell Rebane says TD SYNNEX built Digital Bridge because partners kept asking to integrate but lacked the time and resources, so it pre-built connectors into Autotask, ConnectWise PSA, HubSpot, ServiceNow and QuickBooks Online that a partner switches on by logging in with that system's credentials and picking sync functions such as SKU catalog, pricing and availability, order status, invoice details, PO submission and quote sync [1Rg0jWCs65Y @ 00:05:08]. Sophia describes the deep end of the same idea: TD SYNNEX is integrating its own service management system with a long-time reseller's, becoming part of that partner's invoicing chain [2qmTwyQCa_o @ 00:06:27].

Speed to quote is the second lever. Scott Frell, director of vendor management at TD SYNNEX, says every Scale Computing SKU is preloaded into the system, so a reseller who reaches out can have a full quote on the solution within hours, backed by a triangular effort between the distributor, the vendor's sales team and the partner [WF4x0_79W_w @ 00:01:55]. Rebane goes further: when a deal registration is created on the vendor side for Extreme, Cisco or Fortinet, the vendor sends it over and TD SYNNEX proactively builds the quote, either parking it in Partner First Commerce or emailing it, so the partner never waits on an SLA [1Rg0jWCs65Y @ 00:03:10]. The AI layer is an MCP server partners can wire into Copilot, Claude or whatever LLM they run; Rebane's example is a task firing at 8:00 a.m. that pulls status on a list of 50 priority orders before the workday starts, with agent-to-agent options for partners who cannot build the full integration [1Rg0jWCs65Y @ 00:06:40]. The payoff Rebane quotes from TD SYNNEX data: partners using the digital tools grow 28 percent year over year on average, versus less than 10 percent in some cases for those who do not [1Rg0jWCs65Y @ 00:09:51].

Expansion economics come next: land small, then expand. Sophia's case is a five-person SMB reseller that started ten years ago with a five-day Microsoft migration and now runs TD SYNNEX support, managed services and security managed services, working with the same contact the whole way [2qmTwyQCa_o @ 00:06:02]. Mark Best tells a bigger version: a relatively small cloud support deployment earned enough trust that TD SYNNEX helped that customer secure a 1,350-user managed service covering cybersecurity, infrastructure, compute, storage and networking, a three-year contract worth well in excess of $5 million to the partner [K3d3674aDZ8 @ 00:07:21]. Jessica Ash and Shyla Roquette of the TD SYNNEX high-growth team turn the expansion into a call script: a customer who calls to buy just Copilot should trigger five or six follow-up questions on data governance, Azure or AWS consumption readiness, adoption services and whether devices can run it, which is four or five revenue motions a partner misses by simply taking the order [4NI20Et258M @ 00:02:16]. Jeremiah Barnes and Bo Garrett of TD SYNNEX cite a reseller that learned at Inspire 2025 how to supercharge its Copilot business and grew from 10 percent to 35 percent and then 200 percent year over year, while similar peer resellers grew 22 percent in the same space [fllmKjJXmBk @ 00:05:10].

callout.body: Moves the distributor and marketplace operators use to cut admin time and widen the deal.
items: Complete the one-time ConnectWise agreement linking in ID Sync first, then press force update after every provisioning change so agreement adjustments land without a spreadsheet [Ingram Micro Cloud — ynfBBQclUKU @ 00:03:03].

Start a distributor services relationship small: the five-person reseller tested capability with a five-day Microsoft migration before adding managed and security managed services [TD SYNNEX — 2qmTwyQCa_o @ 00:06:47].
On any inbound Copilot order, ask about data governance, cloud consumption readiness, adoption services and device capability before closing the single line [TD SYNNEX — 4NI20Et258M @ 00:02:37].

sop_steps.action: Pull deal-registration quotes from the portal and connect your LLM to the MCP server.

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split in the channel is over whose logo the end customer actually sees. Steven Andis of TD SYNNEX pitches support and managed services delivered in the partner's name, with engineers arriving on site in either a TD SYNNEX shirt or the partner's shirt, so the reseller keeps owning the relationship [ULy4t5kvUt0 @ 00:14:41]. Ben Elder at Ingram Micro Cloud sells the same move as white-label level 1 support through a 24/7 cloud management service desk working in local languages [M5I7gKJnNwU @ 00:02:57]. Jay McBain of Canalys says the buyer has moved the other way: seven-layer deals now carry seven partners, there is no single throat to choke, and the buyer outsourcing security MDR says plainly, I don't want white labeled, I want to see that company [3uRf7nlQ_JY @ 00:08:45]. Sophia of TD SYNNEX sits between the camps: after finding a large UK partner outsourcing services to over 300 providers, the pitch is to make the distributor the central point, though Sophia hedges that it is not the one throat to choke kind of methodology [2qmTwyQCa_o @ 00:03:26]. McBain's counterweight is that partnering is a team sport where only one of the seven members may ever collect the money if they do it all.

Route to market splits the same way. McBain treats the cloud marketplace as the new distributor: Canalys predicted AWS would crack the top 10 distributors by 2025, and it got there by the end of 2023, with companies now announcing billion-dollar businesses run through AWS alone [3uRf7nlQ_JY @ 00:13:34]. Russell Rebane of TD SYNNEX answers by digitizing the distributor instead of ceding the storefront, citing 83% of B2B buyers preferring digital channels and building PartnerFirst Commerce, prebuilt ERP connectors, MCP servers and StreamOne Ion, while promising people stay behind the scenes for partners who want them [1Rg0jWCs65Y @ 00:01:16]. The InaCOMP chairman runs the opposite slogan, people first and personalizing IT second, crediting TD SYNNEX's Partner Link community and practice builder tools as the differentiator against other distributors [5GVULJyWQFc @ 00:01:10]. Sophia's case backs the human camp: a five-person SMB reseller started with a five-day Microsoft migration and, ten years on, buys support, managed services and security managed services, and is integrating its services management system into TD SYNNEX's, all worked by the same person throughout [2qmTwyQCa_o @ 00:06:47]. Two live playbooks emerge: go marketplace-native for the digital-first buyer, or win on a named human whose small first job compounds into trust and bigger scope.

Whether to build services in-house is the third fault line. Mark Best of TD SYNNEX refuses to call outsourcing stronger, only more viable, particularly in the early years, arguing that a partner's best experts belong in front of customers on sales, pre-sales and marketing rather than in a 24/7 back office [K3d3674aDZ8 @ 00:03:37]. Best adds the distributor will carry services for a period of time, however long that may be. Nikki Meyer of Pax8 runs a dual track: services delivered on the MSP's behalf, or skilling that teaches the MSP to deliver and monetize those services itself, so headcount never caps what the MSP can sell [Ccgwwzx0ld4 @ 00:06:17]. On breadth, Jessica Ash and Shyla Roquette of TD SYNNEX's high-growth team say the fastest-growing partners are not specialists in one layer but the ones converging infrastructure, cloud, security, AI and services around a single customer outcome [4NI20Et258M @ 00:04:01]. Jeremiah Barnes and Bo Garrett, also at TD SYNNEX, soften that line: a security shop concentrated in one vendor may find the market moving past it, yet they say that is okay, it is about strategy, and not every partner needs the same journey, which is why they run 152 model configurations instead of one ranking [fllmKjJXmBk @ 00:06:38].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The biggest firsthand trap in consumption reselling is fraud liability. Drew Simones, TD SYNNEX's CISO, lays it out: under the reseller agreement, consumption billed to the customer is the reseller's responsibility, and if the customer cannot pay or defaults, the reseller owns the bill [8xAn9TMt7Ew @ 00:03:23]. The hyperscaler is neither inclined nor required to waive costs from fraud or misuse of a customer's account or credentials, and Simones warns that many resellers lack the balance sheet to absorb three, four or five million dollars in fraudulent charges, losses Simones calls material and even existential [8xAn9TMt7Ew @ 00:04:17]. Speed is the killer: attackers can run up millions in days or sometimes hours, well before most organizations notice, and every hyperscaler is exposed to this kind of fraud, which makes it lucrative and attractive to criminals [8xAn9TMt7Ew @ 00:02:02]. The exposure scales with the market shift Jay McBain maps: 96% of the industry is partner-assisted whether sold direct, through a marketplace or indirect, because that is how money flows in a subscription, consumption and now micro-consumption model [SwebwmaZR2I @ 00:02:24]. Simones' bottom line is blunt: you cannot count on the hyperscaler absorbing those losses on your behalf, so awareness, early detection and prevention are the partner's job.

Simones breaks the attack down by vector and warns that criminals are financially motivated to keep inventing new ones. Most common is a compromised credential, almost always on an account with no MFA enabled and often lost to phishing, which the attacker then uses to spin up compute or extend the subscription, frequently for crypto mining [8xAn9TMt7Ew @ 00:05:54]. The vector most likely to land on the reseller's doorstep is impersonation: AI makes it easy to forge synthetic or stolen IDs and research a company convincingly enough to pass onboarding, and when the company does not exist there is nobody to go after except the reseller [8xAn9TMt7Ew @ 00:08:28]. The controls Simones teaches are concrete: MFA on every cloud, administrator and console account, no just-in-case access, budgets with alerts at 50, 90 and 100%, anomaly detection, daily consumption review, an AI agent doing that review if needed, and an immediate call to the customer on any spike, because that uncomfortable conversation beats millions in fraudulent consumption [8xAn9TMt7Ew @ 00:11:49]. Russell Rebane describes the same agent pattern on the order side, a task that runs every day at 8:00 a.m. against a list of 50 orders so the partner has current status before the day starts [1Rg0jWCs65Y @ 00:06:27].

The non-fraud failures are operational. Steven Andis says the constraint is not finding projects but finding people, with security, AI and cloud skills in high demand and short supply, and the TD SYNNEX partner survey flags an AI skills deficit as the core challenge behind the AI opportunity [ULy4t5kvUt0 @ 00:07:43]. Mark Best describes 24/7 managed services as everything underneath the iceberg, the systems, processes and maturity that are just too challenging for partners today, which is why more partners outsource parts of their own service delivery [K3d3674aDZ8 @ 00:03:03]. Best adds that vendors measure TD SYNNEX quarterly against stringent governance and certifications, a big overhead partners would otherwise carry alone. Sophia's large UK partner shows the sprawl cost of the alternative: buying product from one distributor while outsourcing services across more than 300 providers in the UK alone, a management load Sophia calls quite intense [2qmTwyQCa_o @ 00:03:05]. On the sales side, Shyla Roquette flags the single-sale trap: taking a lone Copilot order without asking about data governance, cloud consumption readiness, adoption services and device capability leaves four, maybe five revenue motions on the table, and Jessica Ash adds that the customer is buying all of that technology somewhere, just not from you [4NI20Et258M @ 00:02:37].

chapters.question_prompt: How does a software seller list on AWS Marketplace and create, renew, and manage private offers?
chapters.title: Selling Through AWS Marketplace: Seller Setup and Private Offers
chapters.subtitle: Seller registration and first listings, private marketplace curation, SaaS contract private offers, future-dated and agreement-based offers, renewals and upgrades, buyer subscription flow, re:Invent custom-pricing updates, and Ops Squad best practices
chapters.executive_summary: AWS Marketplace practitioners agree the private offer is the enterprise closing tool: a custom contract pinned to a buyer's AWS account ID, with AWS invoicing, collecting, and disbursing the money. Setup is free and requires an eligible jurisdiction for paid listings, a paid listing, management portal access, and ideally a dedicated seller of record account. Mechanics: a five-step offer wizard, up to 23 buyers per SaaS contract offer, durations up to five years, installment schedules, and a worked example where an $80 discounted price nets the ISV $72 after a 10 percent listing fee. Renewals run through agreement-based offers that replace the live subscription. Speakers diverge on pace and packaging: AWS staff push standard contracts, CRM API integration, and future dated agreements, while PartnerCloud argues against bucketing everything under one company-name listing.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every speaker who touches the mechanic lands on the same definition: a private offer is a custom contract created from a listing and pinned to a specific buyer AWS account. Prunal, CEO and co-founder of Clazar, frames it as customized contracts carrying special pricing or terms for specific customers, all inside the AWS Marketplace ecosystem, with AWS still handling billing and payments so no separate invoicing is required [h7liwzzA_-I @ 00:00:20]. The AWS ISV operations walkthrough states it the same way: the customer receives pricing that is not publicly available, negotiates terms with the seller, and the partner creates the offer for the AWS account the customer designates, with each offer carrying its own pricing, licensing terms, and a set expiration date [qWl-wamuA-Q @ 00:01:04]. David, presenting at re:Invent 2024, boils it down further: partners can write custom quotes to their customers through private offers, covering volume discounts, custom contractual terms, and specific payment schedules [K-GonrtXvKA @ 00:02:50]. Tyler from the AWS Marketplace team positions the same feature as the white glove lane, distinct from self-service click-to-subscribe, where sellers control contract terms and payment schedules as they see fit [HU_SJTFHcGU @ 00:02:20]. The shared takeaway for an operator is simple: negotiate the deal directly with the buyer, then let the offer and AWS billing carry the paperwork and collections.

The baseline prerequisites are short and repeated across sources. The ISV operations walkthrough lists three: the partner must have a paid listing in AWS Marketplace, must have access to the AWS Marketplace Management Portal, and the buyer must be an AWS customer [qWl-wamuA-Q @ 00:05:26]. Tyler's registration walkthrough states there is no charge or fee to register as a seller and recommends a fresh AWS account as the seller of record, because every Marketplace interaction ties to that account; sellers told AWS that separating production accounts from the seller of record account simplifies management, separates disbursements, and adds a security layer [w6XECzZOfXY @ 00:01:44]. David's re:Invent sequence matches the onboarding order: sign in with an AWS account, agree to the terms and conditions, set up the seller profile and banking info, create the first product listing, integrate with the Billing API for contract or usage consumption, then start selling [K-GonrtXvKA @ 00:04:52]. On the profile side, the PartnerCloud host walked the horizontal tabs live: a public profile needing only a 300 by 150 logo file, display name, URL, and a 600 character max description, then tax information, bank account, KYC with extra requirements in EMEA and South Korea, service link roles for resale authorizations, and notifications [qXei9F9hLNU @ 00:02:35].

The commercial case is consistent across the speakers: buyers want to consolidate third-party spend onto the AWS bill, and sellers ride that procurement path. Tyler reports the most common customer feedback is love for consolidating third-party software expenses into the AWS bill, plus pay-as-you-go consumption and flexible payment terms, and on the seller side some sellers shared they accelerated sales cycles upwards of 50 percent because the heavy lifting of working with procurement teams and approving software purchases gets eliminated [HU_SJTFHcGU @ 00:05:22]. David layers on vendor outcomes of 80 percent bigger deals, 81 percent return on investment, 27 percent higher win rates, and 40 percent higher deal sizes, and notes customers often buy through Marketplace to meet AWS commitments [K-GonrtXvKA @ 00:02:05]. Prunal pitches private offers as one of the best ways to accelerate enterprise transactions, specifically for enterprise customers needing tailored pricing and contract terms, multi-year or volume deals, and channel motions through CPPO [h7liwzzA_-I @ 00:01:15]. The PartnerCloud host adds a field-level angle: a professional services purchase through Marketplace burns down the buyer's Marketplace commit, which becomes a selling point written straight into the listing copy [qXei9F9hLNU @ 00:14:47].
