sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The build path is identical across demos. Log into the AWS Marketplace Management Portal, open the Offers tab, and hit the orange Create Private Offer button; David describes a five-step wizard covering pricing details, duration, terms, legal documents, and the customer's AWS ID [K-GonrtXvKA @ 00:05:38]. The SaaS contract demo runs the same order in practice: select product type, pick the product, wait up to 30 seconds for the offer ID to generate, set offer name, description, renewal flag and expiration date, then configure pricing and duration, add the buyer account ID, and attach legal terms such as the Standard Contract for AWS Marketplace [2qDBJ9lxIdQ @ 00:01:42]. That same demo caps targeting at up to 23 buyers on a single private offer and treats an Active status as the signal the offer is published and available for the buyer to accept [2qDBJ9lxIdQ @ 00:03:53]. The earlier generic demo shows the payload: dimensions are the features, services, and usage amounts of the software; the seller can let customers pick quantity, designate price, select zero dollar pricing, and add service agreement details, then copy the offer URL and email it straight to the buyer [PVL4069oqC0 @ 00:01:11].

Pricing structure is where the deal gets shaped. David splits private offer pricing into four basic structures: contract pricing with an upfront fee for a set term, usage pay-as-you-go, installment payment schedules where AWS invoices on dates the two sides agree, and hybrids where a contract converts into overage once the customer hits the max; installment dates themselves often become a negotiation lever [K-GonrtXvKA @ 00:03:34]. The ISV walkthrough lists standard SaaS contract durations of one month, one year, two years, or three years, with custom contracts for any number of months up to five years [qWl-wamuA-Q @ 00:02:17]. Its worked unit economics: a $100 list product discounted 20 percent becomes an $80 private offer price, AWS charges the customer $80, and after a 10 percent listing fee the ISV nets $72, with VAT or other taxes added on top of the customer price at invoicing [qWl-wamuA-Q @ 00:10:25]. In the installment demo, the seller starts the contract on acceptance with a 12 month duration, picks dimensions, applies a bulk unit price to usage dimensions, enters total contract price and number of installments, sets the first invoice date, generates the plan, and can manually edit each invoice amount or date [2qDBJ9lxIdQ @ 00:02:43].

After signature, the money and renewal mechanics take over. Customers receive AWS invoices on the third of the month, Marketplace purchases ride on the monthly AWS invoice under AWS net payment terms, and buyer funds can take one to two days to post to the sub ledger before they count toward a disbursement [qWl-wamuA-Q @ 00:11:43]. For upgrades and renewals on SaaS contracts, Chloe Weaver walks the agreement-based offer: open the Agreements tab, search the active subscription by buyer AWS account ID, click create agreement-based offer, set end date, dimensions, quantity, usage pricing, payment schedule, and EULA, mark it as a renewal, then allow up to 45 minutes for the new offer ID and URL to appear [KzcE0ZWyjzk @ 00:01:58]. The companion demo adds that the seller can co-term on the existing end date, keep the current EULA or swap to standard, enterprise, or custom terms, bill upfront by scheduling the invoice for today, and set expiration at least two weeks out because AWS systems run on UTC [MlboB3rLbvE @ 00:02:38]. Future dated offers let the seller pick New Offer starting at a future date with service start and end dates; once accepted it becomes a future dated agreement [xLqQjXa2edo @ 00:01:16].

callout.title: Speed and Renewal Levers Practitioners Actually Use
callout.body: Once the first offer is live, the speakers point to four levers that cut build time, lift renewals, and make listings findable.
items: Use clone to new to replicate configurations from past offers and adjust them for renewals or revisions, then export any extended offer to PDF with one click for stakeholders and offline collaboration [AWS Events — K-GonrtXvKA @ 00:09:10]

At higher volume, integrate with the Marketplace API so private offers go out from the CRM instead of logging into the portal every single time; products and agreements can be read there too [AWS Events — K-GonrtXvKA @ 00:14:28]

Push future dated agreements for renewals: an Ops Squad speaker reports partners implementing them at scale saw their renewal rate go up and ended the end-of-year scramble for unclosed deals [Amazon Web Services — gNv2wvhYkzA @ 00:03:43]

Avoid bucketing every deal under one company-name listing; break offerings into separate SKUs by product or industry so buyers and AWS field sellers can actually find them [PartnerCloud — qXei9F9hLNU @ 00:20:18]

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The first fork is how the cash moves. The AWS SaaS-contract walkthrough lays out two pricing tracks: contract pricing with upfront payment, where the buyer picks quantities and AWS invoices the full amount the moment the private offer is accepted, versus contract pricing with an installment plan, where the seller enters a total contract price, a number of installments and a first invoice date, then can hand-edit each invoice amount or date [2qDBJ9lxIdQ @ 00:02:24]. David at re:Invent treats installments as a bargaining chip rather than an admin setting: AWS sends the invoice on the specific date seller and customer agree on, and the installment date and distribution becomes a factor in the negotiation [K-GonrtXvKA @ 00:03:56]. The catch surfaces on renewals. Chloe Weaver points out that every agreement-based offer is created with scheduled payments, which requires the buyer to be on invoicing terms with AWS [KzcE0ZWyjzk @ 00:01:37]. The buyer-side walkthrough spells out the fix: switch the account to invoicing terms, also called ACH direct debit, by opening a customer service case under Account and billing support in the Marketplace category with company name, contact name, phone, email and mailing address attached [XvBBSBimMn4 @ 00:05:47]. Upfront billing dodges that friction; installments demand the buyer's billing setup be sorted first.

The second split is where offers get built. The ISV operations overview describes the old way, manually entering deal details into a form for customization, and the new way: the seller creates tool inside the AWS Marketplace Management Portal, which lets the partner build the offer independently without being in touch with the AWS team, with a direct ask to reach out if the tool is not working on the account [qWl-wamuA-Q @ 00:06:07]. David pushes past the portal entirely once volume climbs: integrate with the Marketplace API so private offers go out from the seller's own CRM instead of logging onto the portal every single time, and create products and read agreements there too, which David calls how you go fast and go big [K-GonrtXvKA @ 00:14:28]. Clazar CEO Prunal pitches a third lane, working with an implementation expert to launch on AWS in a couple of weeks or less [h7liwzzA_-I @ 00:01:50]. Inside the AWS Ops Squad, the favorite low-tech fix is simply drafts: one team member calls saving as drafts a game changer because folks no longer have to complete private offer creation in one step and can walk away until they have all of the information [gNv2wvhYkzA @ 00:04:12]. Low-volume sellers can live in the wizard; high-volume sellers are told to wire the API.

Packaging is the third fault line. The PartnerCloud host, listing professional services, skipped tiered dimensions like platinum, gold and silver, kept a single monthly dimension and chose to shoehorn everyone into that one option, pushing differentiation into private pricing; by default the whole listing routes through private pricing, and the host is still curious what showing a public price for the assessment would look and feel like [qXei9F9hLNU @ 00:17:19]. David argues for a different emphasis: tap product-led growth with self-service click-to-buy, free trials, request for demo and request for private offer so customers start on Marketplace, become leads and get access to larger private-offer deals [K-GonrtXvKA @ 00:12:16]. Tyler from the AWS Marketplace team frames the same split as two purchase paths, self-service subscription with little to no intervention versus private offers as a white glove experience where sellers control contract terms and payment schedules as they see fit [HU_SJTFHcGU @ 00:02:20]. The PartnerCloud host also takes a swing at big partners who bucket every transaction under one company-named listing, arguing that separate SKUs per offering and per industry, healthcare versus education versus automotive, make the seller findable by buyers and AWS field sellers alike [qXei9F9hLNU @ 00:20:51]. The trade is reach through a public price versus control through a custom quote.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most common dead deal is a link that stops working. The ISV operations overview is blunt: every private offer carries a set expiration date, and if the customer does not accept by then the offer is no longer available, leaving the partner to either extend the expiration date or create a new offer [qWl-wamuA-Q @ 00:01:43]. The agreement-based offer walkthrough adds the clock detail that trips sellers: AWS systems run in UTC time, and best practice is to set the expiration date for at least two weeks [MlboB3rLbvE @ 00:02:38]. When the buyer clicks and hits a 404, the AWS troubleshooting list runs in order: confirm the buyer is logged in to the correct account ID, confirm with the ISV or channel partner that the offer was created for that account ID, and check whether it expired, which the seller fixes by modifying the expiration date in the Offers tab [XvBBSBimMn4 @ 00:06:43]. Two quieter blockers follow: a buyer running a private marketplace needs the product on its allow list, and ISVs using limited listings, products not available on the public Marketplace, must allow the customer's account to view it; only after that does the advice drop to clearing cache and cookies, incognito windows or a different browser, never Internet Explorer [XvBBSBimMn4 @ 00:07:16].

Renewals and SaaS fulfillment carry their own landmines. Chloe Weaver warns that when a buyer subscribes to an agreement-based offer it completely replaces the current subscription: invoices already generated stay untouched, but invoices from the original deal that have not been generated yet are replaced by the new payment schedule, and no cancellation of the previous subscription is necessary [KzcE0ZWyjzk @ 00:02:16]. Timing is not instant either; the agreement-based offer walkthrough says the offer is created within 45 minutes and only then becomes available to send from the Offers tab, so the link is not ready the instant the offer is submitted [MlboB3rLbvE @ 00:03:17]. On SaaS, the create-offer demo stresses that AWS does not provision SaaS products: after subscribing, the buyer must register on the seller's website, and if the product includes consumption, additional usage is billed on top of the upfront amount [PVL4069oqC0 @ 00:02:32]. The buyer-side walkthrough ties that overage to the seller's plumbing, since additional usage is billed on the third of the following month provided the ISV sends AWS metering records [XvBBSBimMn4 @ 00:04:25]. Skip the registration page or the metering feed and the deal closes on paper while the product access or the overage revenue never lands.

Run the economics check before granting the discount. The ISV overview walks the math: a $100 list price with a 20 percent negotiated discount lands the customer at $80, and when the customer pays the AWS invoice, AWS disburses that $80 minus applicable listing fees, which at the 10 percent fee used in the example nets the ISV $72 [qWl-wamuA-Q @ 00:10:25]. The cash lag is structural: customers receive invoices on the third of the month, AWS invoice net payment terms apply, and once a payment is received it can take one to two days to post to the sub-ledger, which must happen at time of disbursement for the funds to be included [qWl-wamuA-Q @ 00:12:05]. The PartnerCloud host hit a different wall during setup: the listing review got hung up because the website had no support section, a professional-services shop with no support component to point to, so the host added one and went back under review with the company profile still limited to private visibility [qXei9F9hLNU @ 00:07:08]. The Ops Squad team describes the year-end failure mode future dated agreements were built to kill: running around last minute at Christmas asking whether a deal is done with everyone's hair on fire, with some partners implementing future dated agreements at scale and seeing renewal rates go up [gNv2wvhYkzA @ 00:03:43].

callout.title: Four checks before any private offer URL leaves your hands
callout.body: Every item below maps to a failure the AWS Marketplace team or a working seller hit or warned about directly. Clear all four before the buyer clicks.
items: Confirm the offer status reads Active, meaning it is published and available for the buyer to accept, and allow up to 45 minutes for agreement-based offers to generate [Amazon Web Services — 2qDBJ9lxIdQ @ 00:04:15].
Set the expiration date at least two weeks out and remember AWS systems run in UTC time [Amazon Web Services — MlboB3rLbvE @ 00:02:38].
Verify the buyer's AWS account ID and, for any scheduled payments, that the buyer account is already on invoicing terms [Amazon Web Services — XvBBSBimMn4 @ 00:05:47].

For SaaS with consumption, have the registration website live and metering records flowing, since overage bills on the third of the following month only when the ISV sends them [Amazon Web Services — XvBBSBimMn4 @ 00:04:25].

chapters.question_prompt: How do resellers and consulting partners transact third-party software and services through AWS and Microsoft marketplaces?
chapters.title: Channel Partner Private Offers and Multi-Party Marketplace Deals
chapters.subtitle: AWS CPPO workflow and resale authorizations, creating offers from Salesforce, reselling professional services, solution-based selling, buyer invoicing, Stackarmor's Service Catalog case, Microsoft multi-party and CSP private offers, partner benefits packages, and CSP billing platforms
chapters.executive_summary: AWS, Microsoft and channel operators teach one resale model: the ISV authorizes a discounted wholesale price, the reseller marks it up, wraps in services and custom terms, and the marketplace collects and disburses, with AWS eliminating purchase orders and partner invoicing. AWS's worked CPPO example turns a $100 list into a $70 wholesale and a $91 customer price, leaving the partner $21; Microsoft's CSP example has a reseller keeping $70 on a $120 sale while Microsoft takes a 3% agency fee. AWS cash lands between the 7th and 10th of the month after invoicing, with buyers averaging 25 days to pay. WeTransact pays resellers 20% or 30% recurring margin. The live divergence is packaging: AWS multi-product offer sets versus Microsoft multi-party offers versus CSP distributor networks like Pax8.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner channel lands on the same skeleton: the software vendor hands a reseller a discounted wholesale price, and the reseller wraps margin, services and custom terms around it before a single customer sees a number. AWS compresses the whole loop into four verbs: authorize, customize, transact and report. On AWS, the ISV authorizes a consulting partner to resell its listing at a discount off public list price, which becomes the partner's wholesale price, and multiple discount types can run for different time windows to cover repeat deals [OhzDVC956Os @ 00:02:15]. AWS frames the channel partner as seller of record, owning the contractual and financial relationship from start to finish, with custom recurring and negotiated pricing [PkznZxwv3eg @ 00:01:05]. Alison Johnson of the AWS Marketplace channel team adds that becoming seller of record means signing the same Marketplace terms vendors sign when they list, after which a vendor can authorize you on a one-time basis for a high-value negotiated opportunity or on a recurring discount across many customers [WP9Y1cRxhAI @ 00:03:24]. Microsoft runs the identical play through its cloud solution provider program: the ISV creates a private offer carrying margin to the reseller, and the reseller keeps the entire customer relationship, including pricing [yC9d52PsuOg @ 00:00:34].

The entry gates are hard and every platform states them up front. On AWS, the ISV must already run a paid listing; private offers built on bring-your-own-license or free products are not supported, the reseller must be registered through the Marketplace Management Portal as a seller, and the end customer must be an AWS customer to accept [PkznZxwv3eg @ 00:01:43]. Microsoft's private offer demo lists its own checklist before you touch Partner Center: an existing public offer, the customer's billing account ID and email contacts, and the name of the customer administrator who can complete the purchase [REkZmdc2hYE @ 00:00:19]. On the multi-party side, Darren Sharp of Microsoft's UK ISV team is blunt that the ISV has to have a transactable solution before a services partner can be electronically authorized to sell it, and Sharp positions the services partner as the agent in the private offer flow [jJAskh3xNOM @ 00:10:25]. Professional services entered the resale lane later: Archna of AWS explains that channel partner private offers originally supported software resale only, which forced buyers to purchase services directly from providers and negotiate with several of them, a gap the services resale launch closed [dkBRJN0WvX8 @ 00:03:09].

Practitioners agree the deal velocity comes from killing procurement friction. AWS's channel pitch is that no purchase order is required, the customer clicks a link to its offer, and Marketplace purchases help retire AWS spend commitments, with dedicated AWS resources for go-to-market and demand generation [OhzDVC956Os @ 00:01:38]. Sharp says buying through Azure Marketplace decrements the Microsoft consumption commitment by 100% of the software spend, which Sharp calls market leading among hyperscaler marketplaces, and the multi-party flow keeps that 100% decrement [jJAskh3xNOM @ 00:07:15]. GP, CEO and founder of stackArmor, reports that finding and provisioning Marketplace software that once took two weeks now takes two minutes, and that customers now expect the firm to play the role traditionally held by a value-added reseller, turning stackArmor into a one-stop trusted source of cloud services [GMejbloTwGE @ 00:03:02]. Jared Smith of Pax8 pitches the channel to ISVs as a way to cut customer acquisition cost and lift lifetime value, because the partner network takes on tier one support, reducing the vendor's support costs too [jJAskh3xNOM @ 00:16:39]. Across all four voices the reseller's real product is trust plus a frictionless checkout, with the software riding along inside it.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The unit economics are taught with exact worked examples. AWS's CPPO walkthrough runs a $100 list price, a 30 percent ISV discount that sets wholesale at $70, and a 30 percent reseller markup that lands the customer price at $91; once the customer pays, AWS pulls the $70 wholesale and disburses the remaining $21 to the channel partner, with VAT or other taxes stacked on top of the customer price at invoicing [PkznZxwv3eg @ 00:10:08]. The same session confirms the partner earns the identical margin percentage on overage invoices as on upfront or scheduled charges, and that the AWS processing fee on a CPPO deal is quoted by your channel account manager, who responds within a business day [PkznZxwv3eg @ 00:13:55]. Microsoft's CSP margin-sharing example runs on different numbers: on a $100 offer with a 50% ISV margin resold at $120, the reseller keeps $70, $50 of margin share plus $20 of markup, while the remaining $50 goes to Microsoft, which takes a 3% agency fee of $1.50 and passes $40.50 to the ISV [yC9d52PsuOg @ 00:02:38]. For resold professional services, Archna demonstrates a 10% markup layered on the seller's price inside the Management Portal [dkBRJN0WvX8 @ 00:12:07].

Cash timing is where operators win or lose the forecast. AWS invoices customers on the third of the month, Marketplace charges ride on the monthly AWS bill under AWS net terms, and payments are disbursed to ISVs between the 7th and 10th of the following month [PkznZxwv3eg @ 00:12:39]. The same team warns that buyers typically pay within an average of 25 days because of their intake processes, so build that buffer into revenue forecasts [PkznZxwv3eg @ 00:12:57]. Leanna Mijarez of AWS breaks invoicing down further: invoicing can trigger immediately on subscription, only private offers can carry a flexible payment schedule split monthly, quarterly or annually, usage products roll into the bill issued on the second or third, and invoiced accounts carry standard net 30 terms with some customers getting net 45 or 60 [vKzo7FINzss @ 00:02:42]. The worked example in that session is a $120,000 contract billed at $10,000 a month. On the services resale side, Archna notes sellers can choose a daily or monthly disbursement cadence, with the customer paying AWS on the agreed schedule and AWS paying out wholesale cost and margin [dkBRJN0WvX8 @ 00:06:13]. The takeaway: price the deal and the installment schedule together, because the schedule decides when your margin actually lands.

The tooling layer is what lets a small deal desk push volume. The AWS partner CRM connector puts resale authorizations inside Salesforce: the demo shows an authorization valid until October 31st, 2025 that supports multiple customized offers, a reseller contract the partner must accept before creating an offer, a markup percentage field that auto-calculates the customer's final price, optional custom terms, and an expiration date before the offer flips to succeeded [pOUxsKDRzvM @ 00:03:06]. The ISV-side connector demo adds comma-separated AWS account lists for multi-account offers and a quarterly installment builder that splits a $4 annual contract into four $1 payments [O_1B3vFfVJ4 @ 00:04:06]. Archna's services resale flow lets the reseller target up to 24 AWS account IDs per offer and attach duration, payment schedule, statement of work and expiration [dkBRJN0WvX8 @ 00:15:00]. Sid of the AWS Marketplace product team shows the new multi-product offer set, which wraps one private offer per component, each carrying its own pricing model, whether pay-as-you-go, fixed upfront or the new time-and-materials option for services [cOyZpsRxxE4 @ 00:31:32]. The buyer still accepts each component individually but approves one total contract value and can cut a single purchase order for the whole amount.

callout.title: Moves the operators actually run
callout.body: Four plays pulled straight from the practitioners who build, price and push these offers every week.
items: Pitch the money before the product: WeTransact offers a reseller 20% for introducing customers or 30% for closing alone, recurring year over year, and only teaches the product after the reseller sees the revenue [WeTransact — jJAskh3xNOM @ 00:35:03].

Push the ISV for a recurring authorization, not a one-time discount, so you can spin multiple private offers for multiple customers without renegotiating while the discount stays active [Amazon Web Services — PkznZxwv3eg @ 00:03:41].

On Microsoft private offers, set future-dated agreements on renewals to avoid service gaps, and keep one-step purchasing on unless the customer wants acceptance before purchase for governance [Microsoft Cloud — REkZmdc2hYE @ 00:02:20].
Put the targeted AWS account ID in the offer email next to the link, because the buyer must be logged into that exact account to see the private offer [Amazon Web Services — PkznZxwv3eg @ 00:08:13].

sop_steps.title: Lock the resale authorization
sop_steps.action: Register as a Marketplace seller and get the ISV to issue a recurring or one-time authorization opportunity at an agreed wholesale discount.
sop_steps.detail: Once the ISV creates the authorization opportunity in the Marketplace Management Portal it is immediately available to the channel partner, so chase the ISV, not AWS, for speed [Amazon Web Services — PkznZxwv3eg @ 00:13:38].

sop_steps.title: Price the offer on top of wholesale
sop_steps.action: Enter the customer's AWS account number, accept the reseller contract, set your markup percentage and attach any custom terms.
sop_steps.detail: The partner CRM connector calculates the customer's final price from your markup and the seller's wholesale price, and lets you add your own terms beside the seller's EULA [Amazon Web Services — pOUxsKDRzvM @ 00:03:06].

sop_steps.title: Build the payment schedule and expiry
sop_steps.action: Configure a flexible payment schedule, set the offer expiration date, and save as draft if details are still open.
sop_steps.detail: An offer that is not accepted by its validity date expires, so set the acceptance deadline deliberately and preview the generated installment schedule before creating the offer [Amazon Web Services — O_1B3vFfVJ4 @ 00:04:41].

sop_steps.title: Deliver the link and forecast the cash
sop_steps.action: Email the offer link with the targeted account ID, then track acceptance and reports in the portal.
sop_steps.detail: Forecast collections with a buffer because buyers pay within an average of 25 days, ahead of the 7th-to-10th disbursement window [Amazon Web Services — PkznZxwv3eg @ 00:12:57].

sections.title: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The first fork is margin architecture. On AWS, the ISV sets the reseller's floor by discounting off list, and the channel partner stacks markup on top. Amazon Web Services walks a $100 list price through a 30 percent ISV discount to a $70 wholesale price, then through a 30 percent partner markup to a $91 customer price. Once AWS pulls the wholesale cost, $21 is left for the partner [PkznZxwv3eg @ 00:10:08]. Microsoft's CSP margin-sharing flow runs the other way. The ISV grants a percentage off its own price through a private offer, and the reseller sets pricing outside the marketplace. In Microsoft Cloud's worked example, a $100 offer carries a 50 percent margin and is resold at $120. The reseller keeps $70, Microsoft takes a 3 percent agency fee of $1.50 on the remaining $50, and the ISV is quoted $40.50 [yC9d52PsuOg @ 00:02:38]. WeTransact's chief revenue officer Juan argues that raw margin is only one of three levers. The other two are back margin, paid retrospectively when a quota is reached, and a services allocation for work such as onboarding or frontline support [jJAskh3xNOM @ 00:31:46]. WeTransact's own tiering pays 20 percent recurring when a reseller brings a lead that still needs WeTransact's sales participation. It pays 30 percent when the reseller brings a qualified deal that closes without that help [jJAskh3xNOM @ 00:32:05].

The second split is over who actually builds the offer. Alison Johnson of the AWS Marketplace channel team describes a concierge model. Once authorized, the partner fills out a transaction request form that captures final customer price, start and end dates, and billing details, and the AWS customer desk builds the custom offer in 24 hours or less [WP9Y1cRxhAI @ 00:04:23]. The operational walkthrough from Amazon Web Services shows partners creating offers themselves from the offers tab in the AWS Marketplace Management Portal. It also warns that the automated path does not cover every CPPO scenario, and partners stuck on creation are told to reach out [PkznZxwv3eg @ 00:04:55]. Sales-driven teams push the work into Salesforce instead. The partner CRM connector surfaces shared resale authorizations, applies a markup percentage against the seller's wholesale price, and calculates the final customer price inside the CRM before the offer status changes to succeeded [pOUxsKDRzvM @ 00:03:06]. On Microsoft, everything runs through Partner Center, where One-Step Purchasing is enabled by default. The demo explains that disabling it forces customers to accept the private offer before purchasing, as an extra layer of governance [REkZmdc2hYE @ 00:01:17]. Each route trades hands-on control against offloaded effort, and operators pick based on deal volume and on where their sellers already work.

Third, practitioners split on packaging. The classic CPPO motion is one product per private offer. It runs under either a recurring authorization, which lets the partner keep issuing offers to multiple customers without renegotiating, or a one-time discount scoped to a specific buyer [PkznZxwv3eg @ 00:03:41]. At re:Invent 2025, AWS Events presenters Sid and Vincent pitched multi-product solutions as the end of stitching deals together by hand. SCC's zero-trust endpoint bundle combines three CrowdStrike products, two Zscaler products, and SCC's own services. Before multi-product solutions, it would have required six separate private offers transacted one by one [cOyZpsRxxE4 @ 00:38:10]. Vincent also cites data that partners with diversified offerings and comprehensive professional services command a 6.4x revenue multiplier [cOyZpsRxxE4 @ 00:15:39]. Under the hood, the bundle is not a single contract. Asha explains that each component keeps its own private offer, wrapped inside an offer set, so pricing, EULA, and duration can differ per product [42TotVxOC44 @ 00:12:06]. Juan at WeTransact argues that the recruiting pitch to resellers should lead with business rather than product. On WeTransact's call to TB Cloud, the offer was 20 percent or 30 percent of the deal before any product training happened, because product learning follows once the revenue is visible [jJAskh3xNOM @ 00:35:03].

sections.title: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Forecasts break on the cash cycle. Amazon Web Services lays out the calendar. Customers are invoiced on the third of the month, marketplace charges follow the customer's standard AWS net payment terms, and payments are disbursed to ISVs between the 7th and 10th of the following month [PkznZxwv3eg @ 00:12:39]. The same walkthrough warns that, because of unique intake processes, buyers typically pay within an average of 25 days, so that buffer belongs in every revenue forecast [PkznZxwv3eg @ 00:12:57]. Leanna Mijarez's invoicing breakdown adds that only credit card purchases settle immediately. Invoiced buyers sit on standard net 30 terms, and some negotiate 45 or 60 days [vKzo7FINzss @ 00:02:42]. Flexible payment schedules stretch the timeline further. The example given is a $120,000 contract invoiced at $10,000 a month [vKzo7FINzss @ 00:01:44]. Fees are also hard to see in advance. When a partner asks how to find out the AWS processing fee on a CPPO transaction, the answer is to contact the AWS channel account manager and wait up to a business day for a reply [PkznZxwv3eg @ 00:14:32]. On Microsoft, rerun the margin-sharing math yourself. The narrated example takes $1.50 off the remaining $50 and says the ISV receives $40.50, but $50 minus $1.50 is $48.50 [yC9d52PsuOg @ 00:02:38].

Most transaction-level traps are mundane, but they still kill deals. The AWS operational walkthrough flags that BYOL and free products cannot run through CPPO at all, because the ISV must have a paid listing [PkznZxwv3eg @ 00:01:43]. Buyers must be logged into the exact AWS account the offer targets before the link works. That is why the partner's email should carry both the offer link and the account ID [PkznZxwv3eg @ 00:08:13]. Offers can also die quietly. The private offer demo states that failing to accept by the validity date leads to offer expiration, and that incomplete offers can be saved as drafts [O_1B3vFfVJ4 @ 00:04:41]. Microsoft Cloud's Partner Center demo adds that the purchase must be completed by someone with the appropriate permissions on the customer's Azure account [REkZmdc2hYE @ 00:02:42]. Before starting, the seller needs an existing public offer, the customer's billing account ID, and the name of the customer administrator [REkZmdc2hYE @ 00:00:19]. Professional services were a long-standing gap. Archna from Amazon Web Services says CPPO originally supported only software resale. Buyers had to purchase services directly, negotiate with several providers, and buy part of the solution inside the marketplace and the rest outside it [dkBRJN0WvX8 @ 00:03:27].

Reseller programs fail for predictable reasons, and WeTransact's Juan lists them. Some vendors pick a market that isn't ready or never check which customers the reseller actually sells to. Others make an offer too thin to bring any value to the reseller's sales force. Often nobody follows up on either side, and the lack of tools to work efficiently makes all of this worse [jJAskh3xNOM @ 00:30:15]. On timing, the answer given is that tactical work with an MSP in an already developed market can show sales within one to two months, while global partnerships take longer [jJAskh3xNOM @ 00:38:04]. Back-office leakage is the next hole. Xtributor checks every invoice three ways: what you bill, what your distributors bill you, and what your books say. Wrong prices, quantity gaps, and missing invoices surface as exceptions, and fixing them pushes billing accuracy past ninety-nine percent [XAc9mTh05so @ 00:01:27]. Partner program cost is the final economics check. On the Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program channel, one partner puts the annual benefits package investment at around $345. Another describes roughly $30,000 in value from a $4,000 package and about $150,000 a year in internal licensing avoided, while a third claims 15 to 25x ROI [RQe8RvOAGRw @ 00:02:54].

callout.title: Pre-Send Channel Offer Gate
callout.body: Run every channel private offer through these four checks before the link goes to the buyer. Each one maps to a breakdown practitioners hit firsthand.
items: Verify the ISV has a paid listing and that you are registered as an AWS Marketplace seller before quoting, because BYOL and free products are excluded from CPPO [Amazon Web Services — PkznZxwv3eg @ 00:01:43].

chapters.question_prompt: How does the Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider program work, and what does it take to operate profitably as a CSP?
chapters.title: Operating as a Microsoft CSP
chapters.subtitle: Direct vs. indirect CSP models, CSP pricing, margins and incentives, new direct-bill requirements, getting started through an indirect provider, CSP agreements, procurement ROI, the commercial opportunity for MSPs, and moving customers between CSPs
chapters.executive_summary: Operators at Pax8, Stratos Cloud Alliance, Manage Protect, Leader and the m365 Show agree on the core CSP play: the partner owns billing, provisioning and first-line support, the license throws off thin margin, and the money sits in services stacked on top. The street split is direct versus indirect. Direct bill now demands $1 million in trailing CSP revenue, up from $300,000, plus a solutions partner designation, a paid support plan and a billing marketplace Stratos prices upwards of $100,000, so Pax8 expects upwards of two-thirds of direct partners to move indirect. Indirect resellers need only $1,000 USD a year to stay authorized and $25,000 to chase rebates, and Stratos insists they earn identical back-end incentives. Friction remains over whether the security score binds indirect resellers, and where enterprise agreements undercut CSP at scale.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator on record frames CSP the same way: the partner, not Microsoft, owns the customer. AppXite describes both sales motions as partner-centric, with the partner running pre-sale, post-sale, cross-sell and upsell plus billing and support [rSX-pZstKp8 @ 00:00:17]. Robert Kofi of the Demystifying Microsoft series says partners explicitly demanded to own the Office 365 billing relationship, and CSP was built so they could bundle services, set pricing and own billing terms [lGN8Dnmwb08 @ 00:00:34]. The m365 Show puts it bluntly for the customer side: buy through a CSP and Microsoft is no longer your billing contact; a 50-person shop gets one monthly invoice and calls the partner when someone cannot log in [LGgw20GtaDQ @ 00:00:54]. Crimson Line adds that CSP drops the enterprise agreement baggage entirely: no 500-user minimum, no software assurance requirement, and aggressive net pricing where the end price is driven by the partner's value-added services rather than deployment volume [pRWl0RalG28 @ 00:02:05]. The structural takeaway is consistent across these four voices. The license is a door-opener and a billing hook; the account, the support queue and the invoice are what the operator actually controls, and that control is what makes the rest of the economics work.

The second point of agreement is that direct bill is being squeezed into a tiny elite. Chris Sharp of Pax8 says the bar used to be roughly $300,000 a year transacted plus a solution designation, and the jump to $1 million could push upwards of two-thirds of direct partners to find a new home with an indirect provider [Xywyds1IfvM @ 00:05:09]. Jeff Edwards at Stratos Cloud Alliance confirms the $300,000-to-$1 million move and lists the rest of the stack: a designation specific to each solution area, a heavier security score, and a mandatory premier or advanced support plan [rV-Q2IVur6I @ 00:03:12]. The m365 Show adds a requirement the others skip, 12 months of prior experience as an indirect reseller, and puts the number of US direct bill partners at only about 30 [LGgw20GtaDQ @ 00:02:00]. Belen Tamayo of Microsoft's channel marketing frames the trade the same way: direct providers must fund billing, provisioning and first-level support, while indirect resellers lean on the provider's platform, credit and training, and break even four times faster [ybzVv-GZvMc @ 00:03:41]. The practical read across all four: if trailing CSP revenue sits anywhere below seven figures, indirect is now the default lane.

Third, the money is in services, not the SKU. Eva Osborne of the Demystifying Microsoft series, while laying out an 8% managed-partner rebate, warned that profitability has to be driven by services and lower cost of sales through scale and automation, with incentives treated as an extra rather than the core driver [wzXR-g6_lxo @ 00:01:53]. AppXite says partners can theoretically earn up to 25% per sale since they control markups, but it is unlikely to reach that, and transacting out-of-the-box SKUs is no longer a scalable model; MSPs layering their own IP on top are the ones with a profitable future [rSX-pZstKp8 @ 00:02:41]. The m365 Show sizes license margin at 8 to 15% depending on incentives and volume and says the real profit lives in managed services wrapped around it [LGgw20GtaDQ @ 00:03:47]. Jeff Edwards closes the loop on rebates: the misconception that back-end incentives get split between distributor and reseller is wrong, because the indirect reseller earns exactly what a direct seller earns [rV-Q2IVur6I @ 00:16:13]. So the consensus operator model is simple: sell the license at or near list, collect whatever back-end incentive the tier allows, and build the margin on the service bundle.

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Getting live as an indirect reseller is a Partner Center exercise. CloudStrategist walks the sequence: enroll free in the partner network to get your MPN ID, sign the Microsoft Partner Agreement, and have each end customer sign the Microsoft Customer Agreement; the distributor then defines how you order, either a self-service portal or orders placed on your behalf [-_TJlxiXPJc @ 00:03:50]. Alex, Leader's national trainer, says the first move after registration is verification under the cogwheel, account settings, legal info, where you prove ownership of the business and the domain; partners routinely stall here by missing Microsoft's emails [GAif9Dapd50 @ 00:08:01]. David Bujaider of Manage Protect adds the October vetting rules: the legal entity name must match your registration, the address must be your primary place of business, never a PO box or your accountant's office, and the contact must be a current employee rather than a former staffer behind an email redirect [Je2jbg9tm0Q @ 00:08:21]. Leader's operational tip is to create customers inside Leader Cloud rather than Partner Center, since the distributor-side record typically auto-creates in Partner Center but not the reverse, and to key in your partner ID correctly because it ties reseller, distributor and customer together [GAif9Dapd50 @ 00:13:09].

The cost sheet for staying direct is brutal. Scott May at Stratos says direct bill requires your own marketplace for transacting and billing, an initial build priced upwards of $100,000, before the ongoing people, resources and money needed to maintain it [rV-Q2IVur6I @ 00:08:45]. On top of that sits the support mandate: the advanced plan at a minimum of 15k, often more, or premier at about $50,000 annually, both of which vanish when you move indirect because the distributor carries support [rV-Q2IVur6I @ 00:12:32]. The m365 Show independently pegs advanced support for partners at about $15,000 a year as the floor, says it ends in January 2027 with Unified for Partners replacing it, and flags up to 50% off that replacement for partners who earn the support services designation [LGgw20GtaDQ @ 00:11:32]. Contrast the indirect entry ticket from David Bujaider at Manage Protect: stay authorized by generating at least $1,000 USD, roughly $1,500 AUD, of Microsoft licensing revenue over a rolling 12 months, the equivalent of selling four annual Business Premium licenses [Je2jbg9tm0Q @ 00:09:56]. That is the spread pushing sub-scale operators indirect: six figures of fixed infrastructure and support against a four-figure annual revenue floor.

Once inside, the pricing levers are concrete. For partners chasing rebates, Bujaider sets the incentive tier at $25,000 USD, about $38,600 AUD, over 12 months, and says a partner sitting just short should bundle more Microsoft services, upsell to E3 or E5, or push longer-term agreements to close the gap [Je2jbg9tm0Q @ 00:16:48]. The m365 Show lays out the NCE price ladder: the monthly term runs a 20% premium over annual list, so $100 becomes $120; annual paid monthly carries a 5% premium; annual paid upfront sits at list; and triennial locks price for three years at roughly 12 to 18% savings versus renewing annually [LGgw20GtaDQ @ 00:05:11]. The same show models the bundle that actually pays: Business Premium sold at $22 per user per month, identical to buying from Microsoft, plus identity setup, device management and a help desk for another $8, landing the customer at $30 on one invoice [LGgw20GtaDQ @ 00:04:01]. Alex at Leader flags a quieter margin lever: the distributor charges no credit card fee, which depending on who you buy from today can mean 2 to 4% more margin [GAif9Dapd50 @ 00:27:02]. Stack those and the service layer, not the SKU, carries the account.

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is whether losing direct-bill status is a demotion or an upgrade. Eva Osborne of the Microsoft SMB team frames the trade plainly: indirect CSP margins are typically lower than direct, but there is no upfront investment to get started, and distributors layer on bill-on-behalf and customer support services that cut your cost of transacting [wzXR-g6_lxo @ 00:03:29]. Jeff Edwards at Stratos Cloud Alliance attacks the margin half of that claim head-on, calling it a misconception that back-end incentives get split with the distributor; he says the indirect reseller makes the exact same back-end incentives as a direct seller [rV-Q2IVur6I @ 00:16:29]. His colleague Scott May adds the cost the direct camp tends to ignore: running your own marketplace, billing and transaction infrastructure can run upwards of $100,000 up front, then takes people, resources and money to maintain [rV-Q2IVur6I @ 00:08:45]. Microsoft's own Americas partner deck lands on the indirect side, stating that indirect resellers break even four times faster and that direct providers must fund billing, provisioning and first-level support themselves [ybzVv-GZvMc @ 00:03:41]. Stratos still keeps the door open both ways, pitching indirect as a scaling runway that could carry a partner back to direct-bill status later rather than a permanent ceiling on growth.

Where the money actually lives is the second fault line. Osborne quotes an 8 percent rebate on CSP sales for managed partners, identical in direct and indirect, yet warns that services margins run significantly higher and incentives should never be the key profitability driver, especially since rebates change fiscal year by fiscal year [wzXR-g6_lxo @ 00:01:53]. AppXite goes further: incentives have been trending down, the latest move swapped them for partner earned credits under the new commerce experience, and while partners can theoretically mark up to 25 percent because they control their own markups, it is unlikely to get there; transacting out-of-the-box SKUs is no longer a scalable business model [rSX-pZstKp8 @ 00:02:41]. The m365 Show puts the license margin at 8 to 15 percent and says the same Business Premium seat costs $22 whether bought from Microsoft or the partner, so the partner stacks identity setup, device management and help desk for $8 more and bills $30 [LGgw20GtaDQ @ 00:04:01]. Softspend pulls the other way, pitching fiscal year 27 growth incentives as a reason to attach assessments and new services because Microsoft is incentivizing that heavily [ziNVpGkDNI4 @ 00:02:07]. That puts the Softspend playbook on a collision course with Osborne's warning to treat incentives as extra, not core.

The EA-versus-CSP line moves depending on who draws it. Carl O'Doherty at Version 1 sets the break point around 2,500 users: above that, EA costs are typically lower unless competitive CSP pricing is put in place, while organizations from 500 to 2,500 users should see near parity on online services [PLfTJs7m4ww @ 00:22:05]. The m365 Show draws the line much lower, saying EA pricing typically comes in 20 to 35 percent lower per seat at 500 or more users, CSP is the call under 500, and under 300 seats CSP is almost certainly the best bet [LGgw20GtaDQ @ 00:07:59]. Softspend argues the historic EA price edge has already evaporated: Microsoft 365 E5 lists at $57 per user per month in both channels, and Windows 365 is priced better in CSP than in the EA [zwXrzaNyZB0 @ 00:00:18]. The m365 Show also reports new EA enrollment stopped in October 2024 and MPSA closed to new business in mid-2025, making CSP under new commerce the default for most buyers [LGgw20GtaDQ @ 00:09:23]. O'Doherty still keeps the EA alive for renewals, custom contractual terms, three-year fixed pricing and software assurance on on-premises servers, telling customers facing renewal to price the alternatives before rolling over.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The direct-bill cliff is the biggest firsthand shock. Jeff Edwards at Stratos says the bar jumped from $300,000 to $1 million in annual CSP revenue, layered on solution designations now required in each solution area you sell into, a heavier security requirement you cannot tick overnight, and continued premier or advanced support plans [rV-Q2IVur6I @ 00:03:12]. Scott May prices those plans at a basic tier of at least $15,000, or premier support at about $50,000 annually, and stresses that enforcement hits at each partner's annual renewal rather than a single October cut-off [rV-Q2IVur6I @ 00:12:14]. Chris Sharp of Pax8 estimates upwards of two-thirds of direct partners could be forced to find a new home with an indirect provider [Xywyds1IfvM @ 00:05:09]. The m365 Show adds that direct-bill now demands 12 months of prior experience as an indirect reseller and that only about 30 partners in the entire United States are direct bill [LGgw20GtaDQ @ 00:01:47]. Edwards singles out legacy partners still sitting on large GP and SL on-premises customer bases as most exposed, because the gold and silver competency route to CSP incentives has largely ended. His fix is to step on the accelerator: lock the solution designation and drive cloud volume well before renewal.

The paperwork traps are mundane but lethal. David Bujaider at Manage Protect has watched partners stall in business vetting because they listed a PO box or their accountant's address instead of their primary place of business, or left a contact who left five years ago sitting behind an email redirect [Je2jbg9tm0Q @ 00:08:21]. He warns that only a global admin can accept the new Microsoft Partner Agreement, that Microsoft may begin de-authorizing partners who have not accepted it by their program anniversary following October 1, 2025, and that partnerships are already being suspended [Je2jbg9tm0Q @ 00:11:52]. Leader Cloud's Alex sees the same choke point from the onboarding side: partners miss Microsoft's verification emails and the process gets stuck, and the distributor cannot force it through because Microsoft does the vetting itself [GAif9Dapd50 @ 00:08:16]. Scott May at Stratos flags the security score as the one requirement nobody escapes, because after October 1 neither direct nor indirect partners can transact CSP without meeting the Partner Center minimum [rV-Q2IVur6I @ 00:15:12]. Bujaider muddies that picture: while listing MFA for admins, a security contact and 24-hour alert response, he says it is not applicable to indirect resellers, with enforcement and the dashboard still pending.

Even compliant partners bleed margin through commitment and consumption mechanics. The m365 Show lays out the new commerce trap: a 7-day cancellation window, then the term is binding with no mid-term seat reductions, so a customer who planned 100 seats in January and needs 80 by March keeps paying for 20 empty seats; month-to-month costs a 20 percent premium, and an expired subscription slides into an extended term at the monthly rate plus a 3 percent uplift [LGgw20GtaDQ @ 00:05:42]. Leader Cloud warns that some Azure resources are quite expensive to provision and that reserved instances only prepay compute, leaving disk, data flow and transfer charges still billed [GAif9Dapd50 @ 00:18:28]. Version 1's Carl O'Doherty sees organizations lift and shift all their cloud spend into CSP without ever right-sizing actual usage, and on the EA side, customers stuffing agreements with incentivized products that become rolled-over shelfware [PLfTJs7m4ww @ 00:09:52]. Leader also points to a quieter leak: credit card fees of two to four percent that a distributor charging no card fee hands back as margin [GAif9Dapd50 @ 00:27:02]. The m365 Show's survival rule is blunt: plan headcount carefully, and if unsure, overbuy slightly, because seats can be added but never removed.

callout.title: Pre-Renewal Survival Gate
callout.body: Clear these four checks before your CSP anniversary date, because operators report enforcement lands at renewal and suspensions are already happening.
items: Audit trailing 12-month CSP revenue and support plan spend against the $1 million direct-bill bar before your renewal, not on October 1 [Stratos Cloud Alliance — rV-Q2IVur6I @ 00:12:14].
Confirm the Partner Center legal entity name, primary business address and a current employee contact, then have a global admin accept the MPA [Manage Protect — Je2jbg9tm0Q @ 00:10:39].

Enforce multi-factor authentication for all users in all partner tenants and implement the secure application model for API integrations [Microsoft Americas Partner Community — ybzVv-GZvMc @ 00:09:59].
Lock customer headcount before any annual or triennial new commerce order, because the 7-day window is the only exit [m365 Show | M365, Azure Cloud, Power Platform & AI — LGgw20GtaDQ @ 00:05:42].

chapters.pull_quote: "The partner earns the margin on the service layer, not the software. That's the model. The license gets you in the door. The services keep you there." — m365 Show | M365, Azure Cloud, Power Platform & AI (LGgw20GtaDQ @ 00:04:18).
action_checklist: Enroll in the Microsoft Partner Network through the no-cost enrollment with your business entity details ready, then use the MPN ID to sign the Microsoft Partner Agreement [CloudStrategist — -_TJlxiXPJc @ 00:03:50].

Verify the account in Partner Center via the cogwheel, account settings and legal info, and watch for Microsoft vetting emails so verification does not stall [Leader Academy — GAif9Dapd50 @ 00:07:43].

Create customers through the distributor storefront rather than Partner Center so they sync automatically, and enter your partner ID correctly to tie partner, customer and provider together [Leader Academy — GAif9Dapd50 @ 00:13:09].

Start capability points with training: two team members passing intermediate Microsoft certifications earns 10 points, and do not burn all customer usage in the first year [Manage Protect — Je2jbg9tm0Q @ 00:15:57].
Sweep the book for organizations under 300 users still on Microsoft 365 E3 or E5 and move them to Business Premium or Copilot for business [Softspend — zwXrzaNyZB0 @ 00:01:19].

Run customer transitions in four steps: intake form, account manager quote, Partner Center approval email with Microsoft Customer Agreement, then a cutover timed to renewal dates [Plow Networks — KkM553ycNrA @ 00:01:22].

chapters.question_prompt: How do enterprises apply FinOps to SaaS and licensing spend, and what does that mean for the vendors and resellers who sell to them?
chapters.title: FinOps for SaaS and Licensing
chapters.subtitle: FinOps fundamentals and scopes, SaaS spend at Priceline and Danske Bank, ITAM/SAM intersections, Microsoft 365 license optimization, ServiceNow SaaS license management, AI-assisted SaaS cost modules, Datadog cloud cost optimization, and State of FinOps trends
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners from Priceline, Danske Bank, Roku, Under Armour and Avala treat SaaS and licensing as a second cloud bill carrying the same waste rate. Gartner's up-to-30% figure is quoted repeatedly, and SaaS now sits inside 90% of FinOps scopes. The consensus mechanics are to build one central vendor list, rank it by spend, focus on the top 20 to 25 vendors, and use identity and SSO data to reclaim inactive seats on 30- or 90-day thresholds. Street numbers include Danske's 3,000 discovered apps against a 600-800 target, a concurrent-license cut from 50 seats to 20 after peak use of 15, Mason's $100K shortfall example on a $1M commit, and soft caps giving 20% free overage. Disagreements center on headline waste stats (Danske rejects the 50% figure), on central versus business-unit ownership, and on whether a tool or Excel comes first.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator on this circuit treats SaaS and licensing as a second cloud bill hiding in plain sight. Chris Reed runs IT finance inside the Priceline CTO org and owns the full tech budget. Reed ranks software as the number-two spend after cloud and repeats the Gartner line that up to 30% of SaaS spend is waste, the same ratio quoted for cloud [hQDjTANIaTo @ 00:04:01]. Eddy Says Hi goes further, arguing that software spend can be 'as big, if not bigger' than infrastructure and using a mortgage analogy to land the point [sIJo4dVD-jc @ 00:01:02]. At the Applying the FinOps Framework session, Amy Ashby of Under Armour and Lindberg, director of cost optimization at Avala, stacked the waste figures. More than 30% of desktop, software and SaaS spend is wasted, 50% of installed software sits unused, and SaaS overspend is projected at 25% [iIwpcQbBkmM @ 00:01:29]. The State of FinOps 2026 numbers presented by Steve Trasch show the mandate has already landed. SaaS now sits inside 90% of FinOps scopes, and nearly half of practices also manage data center spend [O3FqsxJScI4 @ 00:10:51]. The operating conclusion is blunt: a FinOps practice that stops at the cloud invoice is ignoring a cost pool of comparable size carrying the same waste rate.

The second point of agreement is that visibility comes before any negotiation, and that it starts crude. Peter Greenshaw, interviewed by FinOps Weekly, lays out the order: build one central vendor list, rank it by spend, deep-dive the contracts at the top, and run the cycle year-round instead of only at budget season [sqpO85TKjEI @ 00:05:26]. Scott Beasley at Danske Bank, roughly 22,000 employees, shows what that list looks like once discovery is switched on. Over two years, 3,000 applications surfaced, the target estate is 600 to 800, and about 100 new apps appear every month through near-real-time discovery [F-5GIklN_Ps @ 00:04:28]. Reed starts from the P&L and pulls the highest software categories. Each one is classified as usage-based or license-based, and then vendors are asked for monthly utilization reports, a request vendors answered with 'no one has ever asked us' [hQDjTANIaTo @ 00:13:11]. The 2026 trends podcast on Eddy Says Hi names the control point those lists hang from: 'Identity is rapidly becoming the primary control plane for SAS cost management' [byD2FJ-NF0M @ 00:12:17]. That is why SSO and identity data feed nearly every reclaim workflow in the mechanics below. Nobody on the circuit waits for a perfect tool before starting this inventory; the first pass is a list, not a platform.

Third, the practitioners agree on ownership and on where to aim limited hours. Derer Mason runs a three-person Cloud CoE at Roku and insists on being the single commercial point of contact for every vendor. At the same time, Mason acts as 'a facilitator, not the owner' of each contract and keeps the whole function centralized [LF1AK1WypX0 @ 00:20:47]. On accountability, Reed pulled costs out of a single 'core Tech' bucket and pushed them into product cost centers covering hotels, rental cars, flights and packages. Reed then published showback with named owners, explicitly framed as not a name-and-shame exercise [hQDjTANIaTo @ 00:14:54]. Reed also applies the 80/20 cut hard: the top 20 vendors carry roughly 80% of spend, so the long tail is simply ignored during audits [hQDjTANIaTo @ 00:33:09]. Lindberg lands in the same place with about 25 focus vendors, the top 20% of the base. Lindberg's reasoning is that the same hour of optimization work returns far more on a $1M vendor than on a $10K one [iIwpcQbBkmM @ 00:15:37]. The combined rule is simple: one central commercial desk, named budget owners who can see their own numbers, and scarce analyst hours concentrated on the handful of vendors that actually move the total.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: License harvesting is where the hard money gets clawed back, and the mechanics are already scripted. Michelle Campos of the ServiceNow Community ranks integrations by strength: direct vendor integration first, SSO through Azure or Okta second, and custom open API last. The Salesforce playbook then auto-builds a software model and a reclaim rule with a 30-day inactivity threshold. Campos recommends reviewing that threshold and possibly stretching it to 90 days [8mJc7j3DW28 @ 00:03:48]. In the live demo that rule surfaced 572 reclaim candidates, which can be reclaimed one at a time, all at once, or on full automation [8mJc7j3DW28 @ 00:05:14]. Scogo AI ran the same play against Microsoft 365 with a natural-language prompt in Cira CLI, stripping Business Premium licenses from disabled and never-signed-in users. Out of 25 licenses, the available count jumped from 21 to 24. That is three seats reclaimed, including one the presenter had missed, confirmed in the admin portal [hkNjUpPIx6M @ 00:02:27]. Procure IT's module hooks the same identity providers (Azure Entra, Okta or G Suite) to split power users from light users. The renewal conversation therefore starts with a list of who does not need a seat [_PyR6G51QW4 @ 00:01:11]. Every one of these workflows runs on the same two inputs: an identity signal and an inactivity threshold.

The contract math is where these practitioners get brutally specific. Mason walks through the commitment shortfall at Roku. Commit $1M over 12 months, spend only $900K, and you owe the vendor $100K. The escape hatch is a mini business case committing to $1.2M, which may get the shortfall forgiven [LF1AK1WypX0 @ 00:14:06]. The opposite failure bites too. Burn through prepaid funds at month nine and the discount ends, forcing an early renewal, which matters because some of those Roku discounts run over 90% [LF1AK1WypX0 @ 00:15:42]. At the negotiating table, Mason asks for discounted overages, free training and support, and an at-will termination clause carrying 30, 60 or 90 days' notice [LF1AK1WypX0 @ 00:25:11]. Reed bakes soft caps into a standard tech-contract framework originally built at UBS, complete with reporting clauses. Usage up to 20% over the cap is free in year one, and in year two the customer pays 50% of the delta [hQDjTANIaTo @ 00:29:33]. That clause structure converts a surprise true-up into a negotiated, predictable ramp. Together these levers turn every renewal from a vendor-driven event into a buyer-scheduled one, with the shortfall, overage and exit terms written in well before anyone signs.

Rate versus usage is the sharpest piece of street math on the board, and it is where most negotiated wins quietly evaporate. Lindberg's worked example is to buy 1,000 licenses up front and watch the rollout take a full year. Every gap between contracted and active licenses is pure waste. The effective rate, contract cost divided by actual usage, can equal or exceed on-demand pricing, so procurement needs to hear that its recorded savings are not real [iIwpcQbBkmM @ 00:11:03]. The fix is to buy in steps rather than full-year upfront; it annoys accounts payable but saves 'thousands…hundreds of thousands' [iIwpcQbBkmM @ 00:16:36]. Greenshaw attacks the tier mix instead: 'I bet 90% of your organization is just updating PDFs and signing them,' so most Adobe users move to cheaper PDF tools while creatives keep full licenses [sqpO85TKjEI @ 00:09:41]. On concurrent licensing, Greenshaw found peak use of 15 seats against 50 purchased and cut to 20. The heat map behind that cut had to be built by hand [sqpO85TKjEI @ 00:11:09]. The pattern across all three plays is the same: measure actual peak usage first, then buy to that line plus a little headroom rather than to whatever volume the vendor proposes.

callout.body: Small, specific plays that the speakers report returning money or leverage at renewal time.
items: Time the negotiation to the vendor's fiscal year-end (April in Mason's worked example), when the vendor needs to close [FinOps Foundation — LF1AK1WypX0 @ 00:24:28].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The first split is who owns the SaaS book. Amy Ashby runs FinOps at Under Armour with no central team at all: business units own their SaaS, and there is no central tool or process beyond purchasing [iIwpcQbBkmM @ 00:04:23]. Lindberg's shop at Avala went the opposite direction, recently folding IT software into the cost-optimization program so roughly 60% of software spend is now managed by one organization [iIwpcQbBkmM @ 00:05:27]. Derer Mason at Roku backs centralization from the commercial side and is blunt about it: 'make sure you're the single point of contact,' with every vendor conversation routed through one desk instead of scattered across requesters [LF1AK1WypX0 @ 00:20:47]. Yet Mason draws a line that pure centralizers skip, telling operators to be 'a facilitator, not the owner' of the contract itself [LF1AK1WypX0 @ 00:37:12]. That distinction is the real fork in the road. Ashby's model keeps decisions close to the business units that consume the tools but leaves purchasing as the only shared checkpoint. The Avala and Roku models concentrate leverage and visibility in one function, and Mason's facilitator rule keeps the business owner carrying the decision. The operator move: if the org chart will not centralize, centralize the vendor contact point and the spend data first, then let owners keep the call.

The second fight is rate versus usage. Derer Mason plays commitment as the weapon and reports bluntly that 'some of our discounts are over 90%' [LF1AK1WypX0 @ 00:15:42]. Lindberg pushes back on rate obsession. Typical vendor discounts land at 10, 20 or 30%, and 'if you're getting 5%' you are 'not working hard enough' [iIwpcQbBkmM @ 00:10:20]. But Lindberg's core warning is that the headline number can lie: 'that best rate you negotiated actually may cost you more because of underutilization,' so the ladder is to optimize usage rather than rate [iIwpcQbBkmM @ 00:13:59]. Chris Reed at Priceline takes a third path and writes elasticity into the paper itself, with a soft cap where usage 20% over the cap is free in year one, then 50% of the delta is paid in year two [hQDjTANIaTo @ 00:29:33]. That gives operators three distinct playbooks: deep commit for discount, usage first and rate second, or cap the overage inside the contract. They are not mutually exclusive, but they create opposite instincts at renewal. Mason's approach leans toward a bigger committed number to unlock price, Lindberg's approach leans toward proving utilization before any number reaches the vendor, and Reed's approach buys room to be wrong on the forecast.

The third split is how big the problem really is and what it takes to see it. Chris Reed cites Gartner that up to 30% of SaaS spend is waste, the same figure Gartner gives for cloud [hQDjTANIaTo @ 00:04:01]. Scott Beasley, running ITAM at a 22,000-employee bank in the middle of an AWS migration, refuses to accept the popular '50% not being utilized' figure for Danske [F-5GIklN_Ps @ 00:06:02]. On tooling, Peter Greenshaw says flatly that no tool 'scrapes all of that SaaS data natively' into a single pane, and the field's single source of truth is still mostly spreadsheets [sqpO85TKjEI @ 00:01:28]. Michelle Campos at ServiceNow shows the opposite end of the spectrum, letting the platform surface reclaim candidates, 572 of them in one demo, to be reclaimed one at a time, all at once, or fully automated [8mJc7j3DW28 @ 00:05:14]. The spreadsheet camp and the platform camp are not arguing about whether reclaim works; both assume it does. They are arguing about when the tooling pays for itself. The operator read: get the first utilization report out of whatever data you already have, then automate once the reclaim queue runs into the hundreds.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive surprises arrive at contract end. The Eddy Says Hi true-up example is the cleanest: licensed for 100 CPUs, spike to 120, and 'the vendor can true up your bill to that 120 rate for the entire year,' with no true down when usage falls back [sIJo4dVD-jc @ 00:02:38]. Chris Reed warns the same mechanic scales up badly, with a three-year over-license recoup landing at contract end [hQDjTANIaTo @ 00:23:09]. Derer Mason runs the opposite failure, the shortfall: commit $1M over 12 months, spend only $900K, and you owe $100K anyway. Mason's escape hatch is a mini business case committing $1.2M, which may get the shortfall forgiven [LF1AK1WypX0 @ 00:14:06]. Amy Ashby maps how differently vendors punish overage: some bill overages at a higher rate, some cut features off, and some force a true-up or a higher contract at the end [iIwpcQbBkmM @ 00:19:57]. Each trap is set at signing and sprung months later. Under-forecast and you pay the true-up at the spike rate; over-forecast and you pay for the gap you never consumed. Either way, the contract terms drive the bill as much as usage does, so read the overage, shortfall and true-up clauses before the price line.

The second failure family is spend nobody signed off on. Chris Reed found recurring corporate-card charges still billing after employees left: '$5,000 a month, that's 60k a year,' multiplied by 20, plus a $300 charge multiplied across 800 other engineers [hQDjTANIaTo @ 00:09:23]. Lindberg reports a vendor that allowed overage and then threatened a cutoff at renewal, with 'millions of dollars' on the table [iIwpcQbBkmM @ 00:34:27]. Derer Mason's version is pure usage velocity: an intern's logging change cost $30,000 a day, which is the argument for near-real-time monitoring rather than waiting on the invoice [LF1AK1WypX0 @ 00:27:49]. Amy Ashby flags load tests as the recurring spike trigger: 'people kicking off load tests and then I'm seeing all these SAS products spiked because they're all tightly integrated,' and questions whether dev environments even need log shipping and advanced analytics [iIwpcQbBkmM @ 00:37:31]. None of these losses came from a bad negotiation. They came from usage and purchasing that happened outside the renewal conversation, where nobody was watching the meter. The economics check is simple: a monthly review catches the $5,000 card charge, but only a threshold alert catches a $30,000-a-day logging change before it compounds across a billing cycle.

The third trap is data you cannot get and paper you did not check. Peter Greenshaw asked every vendor to adopt FOCUS and roughly one agreed [sqpO85TKjEI @ 00:02:00]. Amy Ashby confirms the gap from the consumption side: consumption SaaS often lacks APIs, overage data is rarer still, and SAM and ITAM tools show only contract-level data [iIwpcQbBkmM @ 00:23:37]. The payoff for pushing anyway is real. Ashby hounded one vendor for months to get an extract on an unmetered enterprise SKU, found a calculation error, and received a credit [iIwpcQbBkmM @ 00:41:34]. Derer Mason's paper trap is the marketplace: the EULA must match the signed contract, because 'you don't want the vendor to have the option to choose' which terms apply [LF1AK1WypX0 @ 00:33:07]. Each of these failures is quiet. No alert fires when a vendor declines a data format, when a SKU calculation is wrong, or when a marketplace click-through carries different terms than the negotiated agreement. The economics check: put data delivery into the contract ask, reconcile vendor extracts against your own usage at least once per term, and match every marketplace EULA to the signed agreement before the first invoice lands.

callout.title: Four checks before any renewal or commitment is signed
callout.body: Each check below comes from a loss or near-miss a practitioner reported firsthand. Clear all four before money moves.
items: Model the shortfall before committing: $1M committed against $900K spent still owes $100K unless a $1.2M mini business case gets it forgiven [FinOps Foundation — LF1AK1WypX0 @ 00:14:06].

chapters.question_prompt: How must software revenue be recognized under ASC 606, including principal-vs-agent calls for resellers?
chapters.title: Revenue Recognition for Resold Software
chapters.subtitle: Principal vs. agent gross/net reporting, the five-step model, SaaS and usage-based revenue, side letters and enforceability failures, IFRS 15 cases, NetSuite Advanced Revenue Management, and how renewals and multi-year contracts affect ARR and retention
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners converge on one test for resold software: control before transfer decides whether the deal books gross as principal or net as agent, and cash never equals revenue. Jobank CPA's ECC case shows a $500,000 GPU resale collapsing to a $75,000 commission once custody disappears, while credit risk and flash title prove nothing. The SaaS CFO, Concierge CPA, and Ledger & Logic all route upfront cash to deferred revenue and recognize ratably. Accounting and Auditing Hub reallocates a $600,000 bundle on $700,000 of standalone value, burying the setup fee in SaaS. Mechanics run through NetSuite ARM carve-outs, RSM's revenue rules, and Ordway's unified billing-revenue platform. The fights: ratable versus consumption recognition for usage commits, with Angela Louu and Devon Coombs warning that overage estimates, breakage, and SSP swings defy every revenue system they pitched.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator who touched the reseller question lands on the same pivot: control, not invoicing, decides whether a resold deal hits the top line gross or net. Jobank CPA frames it as two outcomes - a principal books the full gross billing to the customer, while an agent books only gross billing minus vendor cost, the retained commission [KjWijHo8iMI @ 00:01:00]. The test is whether the reseller controls the specified good or service before it reaches the end customer; if the obligation is only to arrange for another party to provide it, the reseller is the agent [KjWijHo8iMI @ 00:01:31]. The 12th & Norwegian hosts reach the same split with a food-delivery analogy: a platform that sets price and takes ownership before delivery is probably principal, while one handling logistics at the restaurant's price is probably agent, and the agent typically books only its commission or fee [Q0XhS1B8mWE @ 00:16:35]. Juliet at Concierge CPA pushes the same discipline from the software side, warning that ASC 606 is not looking at the word software but at how control transfers, so a perpetual license lands at a point in time while ongoing access lands over time [I8dBdXuT7cA @ 00:14:41]. Look past the label, trace control, and price the deal accordingly.

The second point of total agreement: cash in the bank is not revenue. Ben Murray of The SaaS CFO walks a $12,000 one-year invoice through the books - debit accounts receivable, credit deferred revenue - and names the classic mistake of crediting the full $12,000 to the P&L in one month instead of pulling it in ratably [p4KgISWaH6s @ 00:04:43]. The SaaS CFO's three-year, $36,000 example recognizes $1,000 a month starting April 1, leaving $11,000 then $10,000 of deferred revenue as each month closes [p4KgISWaH6s @ 00:06:57]. Concierge CPA runs the same play at bigger size: Big Tech collects $120,000 on January 1, recognizes zero that day, credits deferred revenue as a contract liability, and earns $10,000 per month as access is delivered; if performance runs ahead of billing, the entry flips to a contract asset instead [I8dBdXuT7cA @ 00:13:04]. Ledger & Logic calls confusing the two the fastest way to fail an audit, because the customer who hands over $12,000 upfront is still owed 12 months of software access, which is why the balance is a liability rather than a win [lYs19gfynCE @ 00:01:01]. For a reseller, that means booking, invoicing, cash receipt, and recognition run as four separate events, never one.

Nobody trusts the price printed on the invoice. Suresh Perryami of Accounting and Auditing Hub lists it as trap number two - never blindly trust the sales invoice, always reallocate total contract value on standalone selling prices - alongside never booking an administrative setup fee upfront even when it is billed and non-refundable [-5y55BOFAKA @ 00:05:33]. CFO AI calls this the heart of the matter in NetSuite: when items sell in one bundle, the price on each sales-order line may not reflect standalone value, so total cash must be spread across every piece on fair value [MAsF2w47iew @ 00:01:24]. Ledger & Logic warns that randomly parking a bundle discount on whatever product feels convenient, without documented SSP, invites massive audit risk [lYs19gfynCE @ 00:03:05]. Dan Colbach at Ordway gives the field version: software sold with implementation and maintenance thrown in at 100% discount still carries three obligations, so the seller must pull each one's fair value out of the $12K total and run it on its own schedule - software and maintenance over 12 months, implementation over four [vPpXI4fjA1A @ 00:10:52]. The operating rule for any resold bundle is the same five steps every time: contract, obligations, price, allocation, recognition, with no step skipped.
